The fluctuations are analogous to those in a non-critical Langevin dynamics model with time-dependent potential and in an Ising model with slowly changing external field.
Renormalization group analysis shows that large susceptibility peaks during transitions occur even away from criticality, and renormalization acts as a classifier that sharpens transitions.
papers.limitation:
Power law fits for avalanche size and duration are sensitive to choices of minimum and maximum values, and the uncertainty is larger than reported, making it impossible to affirm power laws are present.
The model of anesthesia is simplistic, acting only on the input layer by scaling pixels, and is not a realistic model of anesthesia effects.
Feed-forward neural networks are not models of the brain, limiting direct biological relevance.
papers.abstract: Optimal information processing in peripheral sensory systems has been associated in several examples to the signature of a critical or near critical state. Furthermore, cortical systems have also been described to be in a critical state in both wake and anesthetized experimental models, both {\it in vitro} and {\it in vivo}. We investigate whether a similar signature characterizes the internal representations (IR) of a multilayer (deep) spiking artificial neural network performing computationally simple but meaningful cognitive tasks, using a methodology inspired in the biological setup, with cortical implanted electrodes in rats, either freely behaving or under different levels of anesthesia. The increase of the characteristic time of the decay of the correlation of fluctuations of the IR, found when the network input changes, are indications of a broad-tailed distribution of IR fluctuations. The broad tails are present even when the network is not yet capable of performing the classification tasks, either due to partial training or to the effect of a low dose of anesthesia in a simple model. However, we don't find enough evidence of power law distributions of avalanche size and duration. We interpret the results from a renormalization group perspective to point out that despite having broad tails, this is not related to a critical transition but rather similar to fluctuations driven by the reversal of the magnetic field in a ferromagnetic system. Another example of persistent correlation of fluctuations of a non critical system is constructed, where a particle undergoes Brownian motion on a slowly varying potential.

papers.title: SOM-VAE: Interpretable Discrete Representation Learning on Time Series
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable discrete representations of time series that are smooth and provide superior clustering performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SOM-VAE, a framework for learning interpretable discrete representations of time series, featuring a gradient-based self-organizing map and an integrated Markov model for temporal smoothness and improved clustering.
papers.conclusion: SOM-VAE can recover topologically interpretable state representations on time series and static data, improves clustering performance over standard methods, and offers interpretable visualizations that could aid in domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
SOM-VAE outperforms baselines like k-means, VQ-VAE, and traditional SOM in clustering performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST in terms of purity and NMI.
The gradient-based SOM training (GB-SOM) performs better than the original SOM algorithm.
The probabilistic Markov model can be learned concurrently with the SOM-VAE and improves clustering performance on noisy data, such as medical time series.
On the chaotic Lorenz system, SOM-VAE learns interpretable representations that capture the macro-states (attractor basins) while ignoring chaotic noise.
On real medical data from the eICU database, SOM-VAE-prob learns representations that are informative for downstream prediction tasks and provides interpretable visualizations of patient trajectories.
future_direction: Extend the probabilistic component for predictions using higher-order Markov Models, Hidden Markov Models, or Gaussian Processes.
Find more theoretically principled ways to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning.
Learn the neighborhood structure as a graph directly from data instead of fixing a latent space structure like a 2D grid.
papers.abstract: High-dimensional time series are common in many domains. Since human cognition is not optimized to work well in high-dimensional spaces, these areas could benefit from interpretable low-dimensional representations. However, most representation learning algorithms for time series data are difficult to interpret. This is due to non-intuitive mappings from data features to salient properties of the representation and non-smoothness over time. To address this problem, we propose a new representation learning framework building on ideas from interpretable discrete dimensionality reduction and deep generative modeling. This framework allows us to learn discrete representations of time series, which give rise to smooth and interpretable embeddings with superior clustering performance. We introduce a new way to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning and present a gradient-based version of the traditional self-organizing map algorithm that is more performant than the original. Furthermore, to allow for a probabilistic interpretation of our method, we integrate a Markov model in the representation space. This model uncovers the temporal transition structure, improves clustering performance even further and provides additional explanatory insights as well as a natural representation of uncertainty. We evaluate our model in terms of clustering performance and interpretability on static (Fashion-)MNIST data, a time series of linearly interpolated (Fashion-)MNIST images, a chaotic Lorenz attractor system with two macro states, as well as on a challenging real world medical time series application on the eICU data set. Our learned representations compare favorably with competitor methods and facilitate downstream tasks on the real world data.

papers.title: CNN-TFT explained by SHAP with multi-head attention weights for time series forecasting
papers.research_question: How can we design a hybrid CNN-transformer architecture for time series forecasting that is both accurate and interpretable by combining SHAP with multi-head attention weights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN-transformer architecture (CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW) for multivariate time series forecasting that integrates convolutional feature extraction with a temporal fusion transformer and a novel explainability method combining SHAP with multi-head attention weights, demonstrating improved accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW model effectively captures both local patterns and long-range dependencies in time series data, providing accurate and interpretable forecasts suitable for real-world applications such as hydroelectric power planning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW model achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) as low as 2.2% on a hydroelectric natural flow dataset.
The model outperforms several state-of-the-art deep learning models (e.g., LSTM, GRU, TFT) for short-term forecasting horizons (15, 30, 60 steps ahead).
For a longer horizon (120 steps ahead), the NBEATSx model performs slightly better (0.92% lower RMSE).
Statistical analysis over 50 runs shows the model is robust with low variability in error metrics.
The combined SHAP and attention weights provide interpretable influence maps, highlighting which past time steps most affect the forecast.
future_direction: Integration of external knowledge sources
Enhanced interpretability modules
Real-time deployment frameworks
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures offer strengths for modeling temporal data: CNNs excel at capturing local patterns and translational invariances, while transformers effectively model long-range dependencies via self-attention. This paper proposes a hybrid architecture integrating convolutional feature extraction with a temporal fusion transformer (TFT) backbone to enhance multivariate time series forecasting. The CNN module first applies a hierarchy of one-dimensional convolutional layers to distill salient local patterns from raw input sequences, reducing noise and dimensionality. The resulting feature maps are then fed into the TFT, which applies multi-head attention to capture both short- and long-term dependencies and to weigh relevant covariates adaptively. We evaluate the CNN-TFT on a hydroelectric natural flow time series dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that CNN-TFT outperforms well-established deep learning models, with a mean absolute percentage error of up to 2.2%. The explainability of the model is obtained by a proposed Shapley additive explanations with multi-head attention weights (SHAP-MHAW). Our novel architecture, named CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW, is promising for applications requiring high-fidelity, multivariate time series forecasts, being available for future analysis at https://github.com/SFStefenon/CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW .

papers.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Autoregressive Deep Learning: Or, Examining Temporal Decay of Gradient Coherence
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish between genuine generalization and mere memorization in autoregressive PDE emulators? What are the limitations of standard models and training routines in achieving generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces influence-based diagnostics to show that autoregressive PDE emulators fail to learn a globally consistent solution operator, instead memorizing time- and class-specific patterns, and provides insights for improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current physics-agnostic PDE emulators fail to internalize the governing equations, and influence functions provide a diagnostic framework to distinguish memorization from generalization, highlighting the need for physics-based constraints or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive PDE emulators exhibit rapid decay of off-diagonal influence, indicating gradient responses are localized in time and class.
Both UNet and ViT models fail to support nontrivial off-diagonal response, meaning they do not learn a shared feature basis across trajectories.
Gradient geometry is class-locked, with limited inter-class influence, showing that models treat different initial conditions as separate tasks.
The neural tangent kernel spectrum reveals a stiff, anisotropic geometry, indicating that low test error coexists with sharp, high-curvature directions rather than robust generalization.
The models behave as statistical estimators that interpolate within neighborhoods of the training data, rather than learning the underlying physical laws.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based constraints as regularizers or architectural biases to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained as autoregressive PDE surrogates hold significant promise for accelerating scientific discovery through their capacity to both extrapolate beyond training regimes and efficiently adapt to downstream tasks despite a paucity of examples for fine-tuning. However, reliably achieving genuine generalization - a necessary capability for producing novel scientific insights and robustly performing during deployment - remains a critical challenge. Establishing whether or not these requirements are met demands evaluation metrics capable of clearly distinguishing genuine model generalization from mere memorization. We apply the influence function formalism to systematically characterize how autoregressive PDE surrogates assimilate and propagate information derived from diverse physical scenarios, revealing fundamental limitations of standard models and training routines in addition to providing actionable insights regarding the design of improved surrogates.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Linear Latent World Models in Simple Transformers: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How does Othello-GPT encode and utilize a linear world model for decision-making in the game of Othello?
papers.core_contribution: Othello-GPT encodes a linear representation of the board state in its activations, and this representation is causally utilized for next-move predictions, with the world model finalized in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: Othello-GPT neurons encode board state information linearly, and this representation is used causally for decision-making in deep networks, with the world model finalized in middle layers.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT linearly encodes board state information in its activations, with accuracy increasing in deeper layers.
Causal interventions demonstrate that the linear world model is used for next-move predictions, particularly in middle layers.
Attention heads can be categorized into types such as 'my token' and 'their token' heads, which track player moves.
Even 1-layer models can encode linear board states, but only deeper models use this information causally for decision-making.
The linear world model is fully developed in middle layers, and later layers may rely on surface statistics.
papers.limitation: Causal interventions are only successful in middle layers and early games, and may not apply to late games where the model might rely on surface statistics.
future_direction: Using mechanistic interpretability tools to understand circuits and decision-making in Othello-GPT.
papers.abstract: Foundation models exhibit significant capabilities in decision-making and logical deductions. Nonetheless, a continuing discourse persists regarding their genuine understanding of the world as opposed to mere stochastic mimicry. This paper meticulously examines a simple transformer trained for Othello, extending prior research to enhance comprehension of the emergent world model of Othello-GPT. The investigation reveals that Othello-GPT encapsulates a linear representation of opposing pieces, a factor that causally steers its decision-making process. This paper further elucidates the interplay between the linear world representation and causal decision-making, and their dependence on layer depth and model complexity. We have made the code public.

papers.title: EDformer: Embedded Decomposition Transformer for Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Predictions
papers.research_question: This paper addresses the challenge of long-term forecasting for multivariate time series, using historical data.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EDformer, a transformer-based model for multivariate time series forecasting that uses decomposition and reverse embedding to capture seasonal and trend components, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: EDformer is a novel transformer-based model that integrates decomposition and reverse embedding, achieving state-of-the-art forecasting performance and efficiency, while also providing interpretability through feature importance analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EDformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple long-term and short-term forecasting benchmarks.
The decomposition and reverse embedding components are essential for performance, as shown in ablation studies.
EDformer is computationally efficient, with faster training and inference times compared to other models.
Explainability analysis shows that EDformer benefits most from feature importance methods, indicating robust feature utilization.
The model performs well on both high-dimensional and low-dimensional time series data.
future_direction: Test the model on real-life time series datasets.
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is a crucial challenge with significant applications in areas such as weather prediction, stock market analysis, and scientific simulations. This paper introduces an embedded decomposed transformer, 'EDformer', for multivariate time series forecasting tasks. Without altering the fundamental elements, we reuse the Transformer architecture and consider the capable functions of its constituent parts in this work. Edformer first decomposes the input multivariate signal into seasonal and trend components. Next, the prominent multivariate seasonal component is reconstructed across the reverse dimensions, followed by applying the attention mechanism and feed-forward network in the encoder stage. In particular, the feed-forward network is used for each variable frame to learn nonlinear representations, while the attention mechanism uses the time points of individual seasonal series embedded within variate frames to capture multivariate correlations. Therefore, the trend signal is added with projection and performs the final forecasting. The EDformer model obtains state-of-the-art predicting results in terms of accuracy and efficiency on complex real-world time series datasets. This paper also addresses model explainability techniques to provide insights into how the model makes its predictions and why specific features or time steps are important, enhancing the interpretability and trustworthiness of the forecasting results.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-based Time Series Classification
papers.research_question: What novel insights can Mechanistic Interpretability methods, specifically, activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, yield when adapted to Time Series Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders to Time Series Transformers, enabling causal probing at the layer, head, and timestep levels, and constructs directed causal graphs to map information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Mechanistic Interpretability techniques can be meaningfully adapted to Time Series Transformers, revealing causal circuits and latent features that enhance understanding of model internals for time series classification.
papers.key_findings:
Patching early layers (Layer 0) yields the largest increase in true-class probability, indicating strong causal signal at the model's entry point.
Individual attention heads (e.g., Head 6 in Layer 0) have significant causal influence, with patching raising true-class confidence substantially.
Specific timesteps are critical for correct classification, and their effects are non-additive due to nonlinear interactions within the model.
Attention saliency provides observational insights into which timesteps heads attend to, but does not imply causation.
Sparse autoencoders can uncover class-specific temporal motifs, suggesting disentangled latent features in the model's internal representations.
papers.limitation:
MI methods remain labor-intensive, requiring substantial domain expertise for pair selection, granularity choices, and interpretation.
The patching experiments focus solely on attention heads, leaving other components like MLP blocks, residual streams, and embeddings unexplored.
Time series features lack clear semantics compared to NLP tokens, making interpretation of causal motifs inherently more challenging.
Interventions can interfere or synergize non-additively due to the transformer's complex interplay of components, complicating isolation of independent causal factors.
future_direction: Expanding patching to include MLP activations, residual streams, and embeddings for a more comprehensive view.
Scaling analysis to multiple clean–corrupt pairs across classes and datasets to test generality of discovered circuits.
Integrating optimization-driven search to automatically identify minimal, non-redundant patch sets for causal graph construction.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have become state-of-the-art tools in various machine learning tasks, including time series classification, yet their complexity makes understanding their internal decision-making challenging. Existing explainability methods often focus on input-output attributions, leaving the internal mechanisms largely opaque. This paper addresses this gap by adapting various Mechanistic Interpretability techniques; activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, from NLP to transformer architectures designed explicitly for time series classification. We systematically probe the internal causal roles of individual attention heads and timesteps, revealing causal structures within these models. Through experimentation on a benchmark time series dataset, we construct causal graphs illustrating how information propagates internally, highlighting key attention heads and temporal positions driving correct classifications. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders for uncovering interpretable latent features. Our findings provide both methodological contributions to transformer interpretability and novel insights into the functional mechanics underlying transformer performance in time series classification tasks.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Analytical and numerical study of internal representations in multilayer neural networks with binary weights
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the weight space structure of multilayer neural networks with binary weights, focusing on the distribution of volumes associated with internal representations of learning examples. It also analyzes the learning behavior and symmetry breaking transition in such networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies the internal representation volumes approach to multilayer neural networks with binary weights, deriving the distribution of volumes and analyzing learning behavior and symmetry breaking transitions, with numerical validation.
papers.conclusion: The internal representation volumes approach is confirmed by numerical simulations for binary weight networks, revealing differences from continuous weight networks in where symmetry breaking occurs.
papers.key_findings:
The distribution of internal representation volumes for the binary parity machine can be computed analytically, revealing a freezing transition at α=0.41.
The number of implementable internal representations NR and the number of domains contributing to the Gardner volume ND are derived as functions of the loading parameter α.
The analytical predictions show remarkable agreement with numerical simulations on finite systems.
Multilayer networks with binary weights exhibit symmetry breaking inside representation volumes, unlike continuous weights where it occurs between volumes.
The method provides a detailed geometrical interpretation of the learning transition and the freezing phenomena.
future_direction: Study of the distribution of metastable states arising from a gradient learning process.
papers.abstract: We study the weight space structure of the parity machine with binary weights by deriving the distribution of volumes associated to the internal representations of the learning examples. The learning behavior and the symmetry breaking transition are analyzed and the results are found to be in very good agreement with the extended numerical simulations. \textcopyright{} 1996 The American Physical Society.

papers.title: Internal Robust Representations for Domain Generalization
papers.research_question: How can consolidating the internal representation of training data improve model generalization under distributional changes?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that consolidating the internal representation of training data is a key strategy for improving model generalization in the presence of distributional gaps, with applications in unsupervised domain adaptation and continual learning.
papers.conclusion: Consolidating the internal distribution is a successful approach to improve model generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Consolidating the internal representation of training data improves model generalization under distributional changes.
This strategy can be applied to unsupervised domain adaptation by matching target domain distribution with internal distribution.
In continual learning, maintaining a consolidated internal distribution across tasks mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
papers.abstract: Model generalization under distributional changes remains a significant challenge for machine learning. We present consolidating the internal representation of the training data in a model as a strategy of improving model generalization.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: Internal representation dynamics and geometry in recurrent neural networks
papers.research_question: How does a vanilla RNN implement a simple classification task through the dynamics and geometry of its hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that early hidden states in a vanilla RNN form class-evident clusters, but the output layer requires a fixed sequence length to access this information, emphasizing the critical role of recurrent dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The network's internal representation reflects class information early, but task-relevant information is only accessible after a fixed sequence length, with dynamics playing a crucial role.
papers.key_findings:
Early internal representations are evocative of real labels, forming clusters as early as time step 4.
Network dynamics significantly aid classification even when inputs are blank, as shown in Experiment 1.
Classification accuracy is highly dependent on sequence length, even with identical relevant information.
Adding blank rows after full information causes accuracy to drop dramatically, indicating sensitivity to sequence length.
The network exhibits dimensionality expansion and reduction patterns similar to those in deep neural networks.
future_direction: Determining how early classification information can be retrieved from internal representations.
Evaluating the applicability of visualization and dimensionality reduction techniques in neural network analysis.
papers.abstract: The efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in dealing with sequential data has long been established. However, unlike deep, and convolution networks where we can attribute the recognition of a certain feature to every layer, it is unclear what "sub-task" a single recurrent step or layer accomplishes. Our work seeks to shed light onto how a vanilla RNN implements a simple classification task by analysing the dynamics of the network and the geometric properties of its hidden states. We find that early internal representations are evocative of the real labels of the data but this information is not directly accessible to the output layer. Furthermore the network's dynamics and the sequence length are both critical to correct classifications even when there is no additional task relevant information provided.

papers.title: Exploring higher-order neural network node interactions with total correlation
papers.research_question: How can we accurately characterize higher-order variable interactions (HOIs) that change across the data manifold, and how can this be used to interpret the inner workings of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Local CorEx, a method to capture higher-order variable interactions (HOIs) at a local scale by clustering data and using total correlation, and demonstrates its application for unsupervised interpretability of neural network hidden nodes and representations.
papers.conclusion: Local CorEx is an effective method for capturing variable interactions that vary across the data manifold and can be used to interpret neural networks by isolating clusters of nodes that perform specific tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Local CorEx outperforms global methods (Linear CorEx, Bio CorEx) at capturing HOIs when interactions vary across the data manifold.
Local CorEx can extract meaningful HOIs from real-world tabular and image data (e.g., MNIST).
Applied to a neural network classifier, Local CorEx can identify groups of hidden nodes important for classifying specific digits; removing these nodes primarily affects accuracy for those digits while leaving others relatively unaffected.
Dropout increases the total correlation (redundancy) in later hidden layers of a network but not in the first layer.
future_direction: Using Local CorEx to study robustness in neural networks and create adversarial data points to improve model performance.
Adapting Local CorEx as a visualization tool to aid in summarizing complex datasets.
papers.abstract: In domains such as ecological systems, collaborations, and the human brain the variables interact in complex ways. Yet accurately characterizing higher-order variable interactions (HOIs) is a difficult problem that is further exacerbated when the HOIs change across the data. To solve this problem we propose a new method called Local Correlation Explanation (CorEx) to capture HOIs at a local scale by first clustering data points based on their proximity on the data manifold. We then use a multivariate version of the mutual information called the total correlation, to construct a latent factor representation of the data within each cluster to learn the local HOIs. We use Local CorEx to explore HOIs in synthetic and real world data to extract hidden insights about the data structure. Lastly, we demonstrate Local CorEx's suitability to explore and interpret the inner workings of trained neural networks.

papers.title: Fighter: Unveiling the Graph Convolutional Nature of Transformers in Time Series Modeling
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer process input time series data, and what are the update dynamics of its parameters, specifically in attention mechanisms and feed-forward networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper establishes a fundamental equivalence between the Transformer encoder and Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), and proposes Fighter, a streamlined architecture that removes redundant linear projections and integrates multi-hop graph aggregation for interpretable time series modeling.
papers.conclusion: This work demystifies Transformers in time series modeling by establishing their equivalence to GCNs and proposes Fighter, an efficient and interpretable architecture that bridges sequence and graph paradigms.
papers.key_findings:
The attention distribution matrix in a Transformer encoder acts as a dynamic adjacency matrix, analogous to the static adjacency matrix in GCNs.
The update dynamics of the value matrix and FFN parameters in Transformers mirror those in GCNs during training.
The proposed Fighter architecture, which removes redundant projections and uses multi-hop aggregation, achieves competitive performance on forecasting benchmarks while providing clearer interpretability.
Fighter's performance improves with increased hop parameter κ up to an optimal point, after which over-smoothing can occur.
Fighter demonstrates cross-modal versatility, performing well on both time series forecasting and text classification tasks.
future_direction: Extending the graph-convolutional reinterpretation to other Transformer variants such as Conformers in speech processing and Diffusion Transformers in vision and generative modeling.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved remarkable success in time series modeling, yet their internal mechanisms remain opaque. This work demystifies the Transformer encoder by establishing its fundamental equivalence to a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). We show that in the forward pass, the attention distribution matrix serves as a dynamic adjacency matrix, and its composition with subsequent transformations performs computations analogous to graph convolution. Moreover, we demonstrate that in the backward pass, the update dynamics of value and feed-forward projections mirror those of GCN parameters. Building on this unified theoretical reinterpretation, we propose \textbf{Fighter} (Flexible Graph Convolutional Transformer), a streamlined architecture that removes redundant linear projections and incorporates multi-hop graph aggregation. This perspective yields an explicit and interpretable representation of temporal dependencies across different scales, naturally expressed as graph edges. Experiments on standard forecasting benchmarks confirm that Fighter achieves competitive performance while providing clearer mechanistic interpretability of its predictions.

papers.title: From Kepler to Newton: Inductive Biases Guide Learned World Models in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn the Newtonian world model for planetary motion, and how can we fix this problem?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that three minimal inductive biases—spatial smoothness, spatial stability, and temporal locality—enable generic Transformers to learn Newtonian world models for planetary motion, transitioning from curve-fitting (Keplerian) to mechanistic (Newtonian) understanding.
papers.conclusion: Simple inductive biases (spatial smoothness, stability, and temporal locality) are necessary and sufficient for transformers to learn world models, and true scientific understanding requires discovering governing mechanisms rather than just curve-fitting.
papers.key_findings:
Tokenization disrupts spatial smoothness and prevents the emergence of a high-quality spatial map in the embedding space.
Using continuous coordinates with noisy context learning (spatial stability) mitigates error accumulation and improves prediction accuracy over tokenized classification.
Short context lengths (temporal locality) induce Newtonian world models (force-based), while long context lengths induce Keplerian world models (geometry-based).
There is a phase transition between Keplerian and Newtonian world models as context length varies.
Regression models with continuous inputs outperform classification models with tokenization when hyperparameters are optimized.
papers.limitation:
The study simplified the setup of Vafa et al. by using one time-scale instead of two.
Linear probing only reveals implicit knowledge and requires knowing what to look for a priori; a fully autonomous 'AI Physicist' would need additional mechanisms for symbolic extraction.
papers.abstract: Can general-purpose AI architectures go beyond prediction to discover the physical laws governing the universe? True intelligence relies on "world models" -- causal abstractions that allow an agent to not only predict future states but understand the underlying governing dynamics. While previous "AI Physicist" approaches have successfully recovered such laws, they typically rely on strong, domain-specific priors that effectively "bake in" the physics. Conversely, Vafa et al. recently showed that generic Transformers fail to acquire these world models, achieving high predictive accuracy without capturing the underlying physical laws. We bridge this gap by systematically introducing three minimal inductive biases. We show that ensuring spatial smoothness (by formulating prediction as continuous regression) and stability (by training with noisy contexts to mitigate error accumulation) enables generic Transformers to surpass prior failures and learn a coherent Keplerian world model, successfully fitting ellipses to planetary trajectories. However, true physical insight requires a third bias: temporal locality. By restricting the attention window to the immediate past -- imposing the simple assumption that future states depend only on the local state rather than a complex history -- we force the model to abandon curve-fitting and discover Newtonian force representations. Our results demonstrate that simple architectural choices determine whether an AI becomes a curve-fitter or a physicist, marking a critical step toward automated scientific discovery.

papers.title: Amortized Spectral Kernel Discovery via Prior-Data Fitted Network
papers.research_question: How can we extract explicit spectral densities and stationary kernels from pre-trained Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) to improve interpretability and enable downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework and decoder architectures to extract explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels from the latent representations of frozen Prior-Data Fitted Networks, enabling amortized kernel discovery without iterative optimization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that PFNs implicitly encode structured spectral information, which can be decoded into explicit, portable kernel representations, bridging the gap between amortized inference and interpretable kernel discovery for scientific and downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic analysis shows the attention latent output (H) in PFNs encodes the spectral content of the input function, forming a smooth manifold correlated with frequency.
The proposed Filter Bank Decoder can recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and construct explicit stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem.
Decoded kernels achieve Gaussian process regression performance comparable to the original PFN and optimization-based baselines (Deep Kernel Learning, Random Fourier Features) while requiring only a single forward pass, yielding orders-of-magnitude inference speedups.
Theoretical analysis characterizes the identifiability limits of spectral density: spectral weights are non-identifiable from a single normalized realization but become identifiable with multiple independent realizations.
The framework operates effectively in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, with an analytical scaling module to resolve global scale ambiguity in the single-function setting.
papers.limitation:
The decoded kernels are explicit stationary surrogate kernels obtained via Bochner's theorem; they are not exact reconstructions of the PFN's internal attention mechanism nor guaranteed to match the true data-generating GP kernel.
In the single-realization setting, spectral weights are not identifiable from a single normalized function sample, limiting full spectral recovery.
papers.abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) enable efficient amortized inference but lack transparent access to their learned priors and kernels. This opacity hinders their use in downstream tasks, such as surrogate-based optimization, that require explicit covariance models. We introduce an interpretability-driven framework for amortized spectral discovery from pre-trained PFNs with decoupled attention. We perform a mechanistic analysis on a trained PFN that identifies attention latent output as the key intermediary, linking observed function data to spectral structure. Building on this insight, we propose decoder architectures that map PFN latents to explicit spectral density estimates and corresponding stationary kernels via Bochner's theorem. We study this pipeline in both single-realization and multi-realization regimes, contextualizing theoretical limits on spectral identifiability and proving consistency when multiple function samples are available. Empirically, the proposed decoders recover complex multi-peak spectral mixtures and produce explicit kernels that support Gaussian process regression with accuracy comparable to PFNs and optimization-based baselines, while requiring only a single forward pass. This yields orders-of-magnitude reductions in inference time compared to optimization-based baselines.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: Learning Local Causal World Models with State Space Models and Attention
papers.research_question: Can State Space Models (SSMs) learn causal models for world modelling, and what are the benefits compared to Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes S2-SSM, a state-space model that learns local causal world models from video, demonstrating that SSMs can perform causal discovery as effectively as or better than Transformers.
papers.conclusion: S2-SSM accurately predicts future states and learns causal graphs, showing the viability of SSM-based models for causal discovery in world modelling.
papers.key_findings:
S2-SSM achieves competitive or better performance than Transformer-based models in both reconstruction error (MSE) and causal graph accuracy (SHD).
Sparsity regularization is essential for learning meaningful causal graphs; without it, causal graph quality significantly degrades.
The model can adapt to unseen composite environments through few-shot fine-tuning of intervention slots.
SSM-based architectures are viable for causal discovery in world modelling tasks.
The performance of S2-SSM is comparable to prior Transformer-based work, despite implementation differences.
papers.limitation: Differences in implementation compared to prior work due to unavailability of source code may affect direct comparison.
future_direction: Experiment with environments where behavior depends on past observations.
Study modelling of occluded objects.
papers.abstract: World modelling, i.e. building a representation of the rules that govern the world so as to predict its evolution, is an essential ability for any agent interacting with the physical world. Despite their impressive performance, many solutions fail to learn a causal representation of the environment they are trying to model, which would be necessary to gain a deep enough understanding of the world to perform complex tasks. With this work, we aim to broaden the research in the intersection of causality theory and neural world modelling by assessing the potential for causal discovery of the State Space Model (SSM) architecture, which has been shown to have several advantages over the widespread Transformer. We show empirically that, compared to an equivalent Transformer, a SSM can model the dynamics of a simple environment and learn a causal model at the same time with equivalent or better performance, thus paving the way for further experiments that lean into the strength of SSMs and further enhance them with causal awareness.

papers.title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a compact vector representation of an input-output function (function vector) in transformer language models that can be extracted and used to trigger the task in various contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that compact vector representations of input-output functions (function vectors) exist in transformer language models and can be extracted via causal mediation analysis; these vectors robustly trigger the corresponding tasks even in zero-shot and natural text contexts.
papers.conclusion: Function vectors are a compact internal representation of functions in large language models that can be extracted and used to trigger tasks robustly across contexts, and they exhibit compositional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors can be extracted from a small set of attention heads via causal mediation analysis.
FVs are portable across different contexts, including zero-shot and natural text settings.
FVs often encode the output vocabulary of the task but contain additional information beyond that.
FVs can be composed via vector algebra to create new function vectors for combined tasks.
The causal effect of FVs is strongest when added to middle layers of the network.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to relatively simple functions.
The conditions under which FVs can be composed are not fully characterized.
The extraction method relies on having a set of exemplars for the task.
future_direction: Investigate more complex functions.
Explore the relationship between FVs and other internal representations.
Use FVs for model editing and control.
papers.abstract: We report the presence of a simple neural mechanism that represents an input-output function as a vector within autoregressive transformer language models (LMs). Using causal mediation analysis on a diverse range of in-context-learning (ICL) tasks, we find that a small number attention heads transport a compact representation of the demonstrated task, which we call a function vector (FV). FVs are robust to changes in context, i.e., they trigger execution of the task on inputs such as zero-shot and natural text settings that do not resemble the ICL contexts from which they are collected. We test FVs across a range of tasks, models, and layers and find strong causal effects across settings in middle layers. We investigate the internal structure of FVs and find while that they often contain information that encodes the output space of the function, this information alone is not sufficient to reconstruct an FV. Finally, we test semantic vector composition in FVs, and find that to some extent they can be summed to create vectors that trigger new complex tasks. Our findings show that compact, causal internal vector representations of function abstractions can be explicitly extracted from LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://functions.baulab.info.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
