future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: LLMs learn governing principles of dynamical systems, revealing an in-context neural scaling law
papers.research_question: Can LLMs learn the governing principles of dynamical systems from in-context data, and does the accuracy of learned rules scale with context length?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can learn the probabilistic transition rules of various dynamical systems from in-context data without fine-tuning, and the accuracy of the learned rules follows a power-law scaling with context length, revealing an in-context neural scaling law.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs can accurately recover the probabilistic transition rules underlying deterministic, chaotic, and stochastic time series when provided with sufficient context, and this learning follows an in-context scaling law.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs (LLaMA-13b, LLaMA-70b) can accurately predict the next state in time series from stochastic, chaotic, continuous, and discrete dynamical systems without any fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
The discrepancy between the learned transition rules and ground truth decreases as a power law with the length of the observed time series, indicating an in-context neural scaling law.
The introduced Hierarchy-PDF algorithm efficiently extracts probability density functions for multi-digit numbers from LLM predictions.
For deterministic systems, the squared deviations from the mean (SDM) loss is more stable than the Bhattacharyya distance for capturing learning dynamics.
LLMs can learn both the mean and variance of next-state distributions for stochastic systems, as demonstrated on the noisy logistic map and geometric Brownian motion.
papers.limitation:
Although unlikely, the possibility of data leakage (memorization) cannot be completely ruled out and requires rigorous testing in future work.
The study does not evaluate newer models like LLaMA-3 due to time and computational constraints, limiting the comprehensiveness of the findings.
future_direction: Investigating how LLMs encode spatio-temporal features in stochastic dynamical time series and how they represent the learned transition rules.
Examining how LLMs perform subtasks necessary for learning stochastic dynamical systems, such as collecting Markovian transition statistics from discrete data and performing density estimation.
Assessing to what extent training on natural language enhances a transformer's mathematical ability to in-context learn dynamical systems, and vice-versa.
papers.abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) are surprisingly effective at performing zero-shot tasks, including time-series forecasting. However, understanding the mechanisms behind such capabilities remains highly challenging due to the complexity of the models. We study LLMs' ability to extrapolate the behavior of dynamical systems whose evolution is governed by principles of physical interest. Our results show that LLaMA 2, a language model trained primarily on texts, achieves accurate predictions of dynamical system time series without fine-tuning or prompt engineering. Moreover, the accuracy of the learned physical rules increases with the length of the input context window, revealing an in-context version of neural scaling law. Along the way, we present a flexible and efficient algorithm for extracting probability density functions of multi-digit numbers directly from LLMs.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: FocusLearn: Fully-Interpretable, High-Performance Modular Neural Networks for Time Series
papers.research_question: How to build a fully-interpretable modular neural network for time series that matches or surpasses the predictive performance of non-interpretable deep networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FocusLearn, a fully-interpretable modular neural network for time series that uses attention for feature selection and node bootstrapping to achieve predictive performance comparable to non-interpretable deep networks.
papers.conclusion: FocusLearn achieves interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art non-interpretable models on time series tasks.
papers.key_findings:
FocusLearn outperforms interpretable models (NAM and SPAM) on both regression and classification tasks across multiple metrics.
FocusLearn matches or surpasses the performance of non-interpretable models (LSTM and XGBoost) on the tested datasets.
The Attention-based Node Bootstrapping (ANB) and Attention-based Feature Selection (AFS) components are effective in improving predictive performance.
FocusLearn provides NAM-style interpretability with feature contribution plots.
Selecting a subset of features via AFS improves accuracy compared to using all features.
future_direction: Evaluate trade-offs such as the number of modules and feature interactions in practice.
Investigate the possibility of using attention to create higher-order feature interactions for implementation into a single network module.
Investigate the practical value of the explanations provided and how they may inform model intervention.
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series have had many applications in areas from healthcare and finance to meteorology and life sciences. Although deep neural networks have shown excellent predictive performance for time series, they have been criticised for being non-interpretable. Neural Additive Models, however, are known to be fully-interpretable by construction, but may achieve far lower predictive performance than deep networks when applied to time series. This paper introduces FocusLearn, a fully-interpretable modular neural network capable of matching or surpassing the predictive performance of deep networks trained on multivariate time series. In FocusLearn, a recurrent neural network learns the temporal dependencies in the data, while a multi-headed attention layer learns to weight selected features while also suppressing redundant features. Modular neural networks are then trained in parallel and independently, one for each selected feature. This modular approach allows the user to inspect how features influence outcomes in the exact same way as with additive models. Experimental results show that this new approach outperforms additive models in both regression and classification of time series tasks, achieving predictive performance that is comparable to state-of-the-art, non-interpretable deep networks applied to time series.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Extracting Interpretable Local and Global Representations from Attention on Time Series
papers.research_question: How can interpretable local and global representations be extracted from transformer attention mechanisms for time series data?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents two transformer attention-based interpretability methods (LASA and GCR) for time series data, providing a framework for local abstraction and global representation that improves interpretability/complexity while maintaining performance similar to the baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the presented methods are effective for extracting interpretable local and global representations from attention on time series data, and provides guidance for their application.
papers.key_findings:
The presented LASA and GCR approaches demonstrate a significant improvement in interpretability/complexity while capturing many core decisions and maintaining similar performance to the baseline model.
The methods provide a comprehensive framework for both local and global interpretation of attention on time series data.
Experiments on univariate datasets from the UCR UEA repository show the efficacy of the approaches, with extensive hyperparameter analysis.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is currently only adapted to univariate data; multivariate data opens up further challenges, e.g., differentiating attention between sequences and/or considering cross-sequential influence.
future_direction: Extending the methods to handle multivariate time series data.
papers.abstract: This paper targets two transformer attention based interpretability methods working with local abstraction and global representation, in the context of time series data. We distinguish local and global contexts, and provide a comprehensive framework for both general interpretation options. We discuss their specific instantiation via different methods in detail, also outlining their respective computational implementation and abstraction variants. Furthermore, we provide extensive experimentation demonstrating the efficacy of the presented approaches. In particular, we perform our experiments using a selection of univariate datasets from the UCR UEA time series repository where we both assess the performance of the proposed approaches, as well as their impact on explainability and interpretability/complexity. Here, with an extensive analysis of hyperparameters, the presented approaches demonstrate an significant improvement in interpretability/complexity, while capturing many core decisions of and maintaining a similar performance to the baseline model. Finally, we draw general conclusions outlining and guiding the application of the presented methods.

papers.title: Smooth embeddings in contracting recurrent networks driven by regular dynamics: A synthesis for neural representation
papers.research_question: Why do low-dimensional sensory manifolds emerge in recurrent circuits, and what determines their geometry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical account showing that contracting recurrent networks driven by low-dimensional sensory dynamics generically develop smooth internal manifolds that embed the sensory dynamics, with explicit dimensionality requirements and a prediction-separation property linking geometry to predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: The results provide a mechanistic account of why low-dimensional sensory manifolds emerge in recurrent circuits and how prediction constrains their resolution, grounded in dynamical systems embedding theory and consistent with empirical findings on cortical population dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Contracting recurrent networks develop smooth internal manifolds that embed low-dimensional sensory dynamics.
The required hidden dimension is modest: N > 2d suffices (e.g., N≥3 for a circle, N≥5 for a two-frequency torus).
A prediction-separation result links representational geometry to predictive performance: if prediction error is small, states with different futures must be separated in neural state space.
Numerical experiments with trained tanh RNNs recover ring- and torus-shaped hidden manifolds with expected topology, and state separation improves when N crosses the 2d+1 threshold.
Training pushes networks beyond strict contraction, yet manifold recovery persists, indicating the conditions are sufficient but not necessary.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical conditions are sufficient but not necessary, as numerical experiments show embedding persists beyond strict contraction.
The analysis is specialized to regular, low-dimensional sensory dynamics (circles and tori), and may not extend to chaotic or high-dimensional dynamics.
future_direction: Investigating whether predictive processing circuits satisfy the contraction conditions required by the theory.
Formally connecting the Bayesian and geometric accounts of sensory representation.
Exploring the biological substrate for contraction, such as precision-weighting mechanisms in predictive processing.
papers.abstract: Recurrent neural networks trained for time-series prediction often develop latent trajectories that preserve qualitative structure of the dynamical systems generating their inputs. Recent empirical work has documented topology-preserving latent organization in trained recurrent models, and recent theoretical results in reservoir computing establish conditions under which the synchronization map is an embedding. Here we synthesize these threads into a unified account of when contracting recurrent networks yield smooth, topology-preserving internal representations for a broad and biologically relevant class of inputs: regular dynamics on invariant circles and tori. Our contribution is an integrated framework that assembles (i) generalized synchronization and embedding guarantees for contracting reservoirs, (ii) regularity mechanisms ensuring differentiability of the synchronization map under mild constraints, and (iii) a base-system viewpoint in which the invariant manifold generating the input stream is treated as the driving system. In this regular setting, the conditions commonly viewed as restrictive in chaotic-attractor analyses become mild and readily satisfied by standard contractive architectures. The framework clarifies how representational content in recurrent circuits is inherently historical: the network state encodes finite windows of input history rather than instantaneous stimuli. By consolidating disparate empirical and theoretical results under common assumptions, the synthesis yields concrete, testable expectations about when prediction-trained recurrent circuits should (or should not) form smooth latent embeddings and how required state dimension scales with the intrinsic dimension of the driving dynamics.

papers.title: Benchmarking Attention-Based Interpretability of Deep Learning in Multivariate Time Series Predictions
papers.research_question: How well do attention-based deep learning models perform in terms of prediction accuracy and interpretability correctness on multivariate time series forecasting tasks, and can they correctly identify underlying causal relationships in synthetic datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper designs a novel benchmark of synthetic datasets with transparent underlying generating processes to evaluate attention-based deep learning models for multivariate time series forecasting. It finds that while most models have satisfying prediction performance, they often fail to provide correct interpretability, with IMV-LSTM being the only model that achieves both good prediction and correct interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that attention-based models often learn to predict without understanding the underlying data generating process, and only IMV-LSTM provides correct interpretability for most datasets. The benchmark highlights the need for more stable and faithful interpretability in neural architectures for time series.
papers.key_findings:
Most attention-based models (seq2graph, TCDF, DA-RNN) fail to provide correct interpretability of the underlying data generating process, even when prediction performance is good.
IMV-LSTM is the only model that provides both satisfying prediction performance and correct interpretability for most synthetic datasets.
Interpretability correctness of IMV-LSTM increases with dataset complexity, as seen in statistical and mechanistic models (Ising model and Logistic map).
Models like seq2graph show low confidence in their interpretability, with attention weights often biased and having high variance.
TCDF model can correctly identify causality when it does, but it fails to do so consistently across experiments and datasets.
papers.limitation: The experimental settings are mainly focused on multivariate time series single output forecasting tasks and specific well-known generative processes, which may not cover all real-world domains.
future_direction: Extend experimental settings to other multivariate prediction tasks, including multi-input/multi-output classification and forecasting settings.
Incorporate real-world datasets from various domains into the benchmark.
papers.abstract: The adaptation of deep learning models within safety-critical systems cannot rely only on good prediction performance but needs to provide interpretable and robust explanations for their decisions. When modeling complex sequences, attention mechanisms are regarded as the established approach to support deep neural networks with intrinsic interpretability. This paper focuses on the emerging trend of specifically designing diagnostic datasets for understanding the inner workings of attention mechanism based deep learning models for multivariate forecasting tasks. We design a novel benchmark of synthetically designed datasets with the transparent underlying generating process of multiple time series interactions with increasing complexity. The benchmark enables empirical evaluation of the performance of attention based deep neural networks in three different aspects: (i) prediction performance score, (ii) interpretability correctness, (iii) sensitivity analysis. Our analysis shows that although most models have satisfying and stable prediction performance results, they often fail to give correct interpretability. The only model with both a satisfying performance score and correct interpretability is IMV-LSTM, capturing both autocorrelations and crosscorrelations between multiple time series. Interestingly, while evaluating IMV-LSTM on simulated data from statistical and mechanistic models, the correctness of interpretability increases with more complex datasets.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: FIGNN: Feature-Specific Interpretability for Graph Neural Network Surrogate Models
papers.research_question: How can we design a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that provides feature-specific interpretability for multivariate prediction tasks on unstructured grids in scientific applications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-specific interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN) architecture with independent Top-K pooling masks per output variable and an error-budget regularization term to align interpretability with predictive error, enabling localized, feature-wise attribution in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.conclusion: FIGNN provides a balance between interpretability and predictive performance, offering domain experts detailed insights into feature-specific contributions to prediction accuracy in scientific surrogate modeling.
papers.key_findings:
FIGNN provides feature-specific interpretability masks that highlight physically meaningful spatial regions for each predicted variable, such as frontal boundaries in climate data and recirculation zones in fluid flow.
The error budget regularization effectively localizes prediction errors within the masked regions, with stronger regularization increasing error concentration at the cost of slightly reduced predictive accuracy.
FIGNN maintains competitive predictive performance compared to baseline GNN models on both atmospheric (SPEEDY) and fluid dynamics (BFS) datasets.
The method generalizes across distinct physical domains (climate and fluid dynamics) with different mesh types and governing equations.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence and error localization) and predictive accuracy, controllable via the regularization parameter λ.
papers.limitation:
Error accumulation in multi-step rollouts leads to deteriorating prediction quality over long time horizons.
There is a trade-off between interpretability (mask coherence) and predictive accuracy, where higher regularization improves error localization but increases final loss.
future_direction: Extending the framework to spatially three-dimensional settings.
Real-time adaptive interpretability.
Uncertainty quantification strategies.
Using FIGNN for inverse problems like super-resolution, control, and optimization.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel graph neural network (GNN) architecture, the Feature-specific Interpretable Graph Neural Network (FIGNN), designed to enhance the interpretability of deep learning surrogate models defined on unstructured grids in scientific applications. Traditional GNNs often obscure the distinct spatial influences of different features in multivariate prediction tasks. FIGNN addresses this limitation by introducing a feature-specific pooling strategy, which enables independent attribution of spatial importance for each predicted variable. Additionally, a mask-based regularization term is incorporated into the training objective to explicitly encourage alignment between interpretability and predictive error, promoting localized attribution of model performance. The method is evaluated for surrogate modeling of two physically distinct systems: the SPEEDY atmospheric circulation model and the backward-facing step (BFS) fluid dynamics benchmark. Results demonstrate that FIGNN achieves competitive predictive performance while revealing physically meaningful spatial patterns unique to each feature. Analysis of rollout stability, feature-wise error budgets, and spatial mask overlays confirm the utility of FIGNN as a general-purpose framework for interpretable surrogate modeling in complex physical domains.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Why Attention Fails: The Degeneration of Transformers into MLPs in Time Series Forecasting
papers.research_question: Why do transformers underperform in time series forecasting, and why does the attention mechanism degenerate into MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that in time series transformers, attention mechanisms degenerate into MLPs because linear embeddings fail to provide a well-structured latent space, rendering attention ineffective.
papers.conclusion: The failure of attention in time series transformers is due to inadequate representation learning from linear embeddings, and future improvements should focus on learning better latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer blocks in time series models often degenerate into MLPs, with attention contributing minimally to performance.
Replacing attention matrices with zero, identity, or average matrices does not significantly affect model performance.
Perturbing the attention module has little impact, while perturbing the FFN module degrades performance, indicating that FFN is more critical.
Positional encoding is not effectively utilized in time series transformers, unlike in Vision Transformers (ViT).
Linear embedding layers are ineffective and unnecessary for time series data, as they fail to enable proper representation learning.
papers.limitation:
The degradation phenomenon may extend to other domains like classification and imputation, requiring further investigation.
Interpreting attention weights in time series data is complex due to lack of human comprehensibility, necessitating new metrics.
future_direction: Focus on improving representation learning before refining attention mechanisms.
Develop novel embeddings, such as using VQ-VAE or encoder-decoder architectures, for better latent spaces.
Create a new metric or benchmark to assess the influence of attention in time series models.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based architectures achieved high performance in natural language processing and computer vision, yet many studies have shown that they have not demonstrated a clear advantage in time series forecasting and even underperform simple linear baselines in some cases. However, most of these studies have not thoroughly explored the reasons behind the failure of transformers. To better understand time-series transformers(TST), we designed a series of experiments, progressively modifying transformers into MLPs to investigate the impact of the attention mechanism. Surprisingly, transformer blocks often degenerate into simple MLPs in existing time-series transformers. We designed a interpretable dataset to investigate the reasons behind the failure of the attention mechanism and revealed that the attention mechanism is not working in the expected way. We theoretically analyzed the reasons behind this phenomenon, demonstrating that the current embedding methods fail to allow transformers to function in a well-structured latent space, and further analyzed the deeper underlying causes of the failure of embedding.

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: Text-Trained LLMs Can Zero-Shot Extrapolate PDE Dynamics, Revealing a Three-Stage In-Context Learning Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can text-trained LLMs zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and what is the in-context learning mechanism behind this capability?
papers.core_contribution: Text-trained LLMs can zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a three-stage progression from syntax imitation to exploratory high-entropy phase to confident prediction.
papers.conclusion: Text-trained LLMs exhibit emergent zero-shot capability to extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a consistent three-stage progression, revealing inductive biases analogous to numerical methods.
papers.key_findings:
One-step prediction accuracy improves with longer temporal context but degrades with finer spatial discretization.
Multi-step rollouts show algebraic error growth with time horizon, similar to classical numerical solvers.
Token-level entropy analysis reveals a three-stage ICL progression: syntax imitation, exploratory high-entropy phase, and confident prediction.
LLMs can sustain coherent multi-step rollouts for nonlinear PDEs like Allen-Cahn and wave equations.
The three-stage progression is consistent across model sizes and PDE types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities across a range of tasks, including zero-shot time-series forecasting. We show that text-trained foundation models can accurately extrapolate spatiotemporal dynamics from discretized partial differential equation (PDE) solutions without fine-tuning or natural language prompting. Predictive accuracy improves with longer temporal contexts but degrades at finer spatial discretizations. In multi-step rollouts, where the model recursively predicts future spatial states over multiple time steps, errors grow algebraically with the time horizon, reminiscent of global error accumulation in classical finite-difference solvers. We interpret these trends as in-context neural scaling laws, where prediction quality varies predictably with both context length and output length. To better understand how LLMs are able to internally process PDE solutions so as to accurately roll them out, we analyze token-level output distributions and uncover a consistent three-stage ICL progression: beginning with syntactic pattern imitation, transitioning through an exploratory high-entropy phase, and culminating in confident, numerically grounded predictions.

papers.title: Translation Equivariant Transformer Neural Processes
papers.research_question: How to incorporate translation equivariance into transformer neural processes to improve their performance on spatio-temporal data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces translation equivariant transformer neural processes (TE-TNPs) by developing translation equivariant attention mechanisms, improving performance on spatio-temporal tasks.
papers.conclusion: TE-TNPs and TE-PT-TNPs are effective and versatile models that incorporate translation equivariance, performing on par or better than state-of-the-art NPs, though with increased computational cost.
papers.key_findings:
TE-TNPs outperform non-translation-equivariant TNPs and other NP baselines on synthetic 1-D regression, especially when test data is shifted.
TE-PT-TNPs achieve state-of-the-art performance on image completion tasks with MNIST and CIFAR10.
TE-PT-TNPs significantly outperform other models on Kolmogorov flow and environmental data modelling.
Translation equivariance helps models generalize to inputs outside the training range.
Dynamically updating input locations improves performance for complex input distributions.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational cost due to passing input locations through attention mechanisms at each layer.
Initialization of pseudo-locations in TE-PT-TNPs can lead to poor performance in pathological cases.
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of neural processes (NPs) in modelling posterior prediction maps -- the mapping from data to posterior predictive distributions -- has significantly improved since their inception. This improvement can be attributed to two principal factors: (1) advancements in the architecture of permutation invariant set functions, which are intrinsic to all NPs; and (2) leveraging symmetries present in the true posterior predictive map, which are problem dependent. Transformers are a notable development in permutation invariant set functions, and their utility within NPs has been demonstrated through the family of models we refer to as TNPs. Despite significant interest in TNPs, little attention has been given to incorporating symmetries. Notably, the posterior prediction maps for data that are stationary -- a common assumption in spatio-temporal modelling -- exhibit translation equivariance. In this paper, we introduce of a new family of translation equivariant TNPs that incorporate translation equivariance. Through an extensive range of experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of TE-TNPs relative to their non-translation-equivariant counterparts and other NP baselines.

papers.title: Explainable Prediction of Economic Time Series Using IMFs and Neural Networks
papers.research_question: This study investigates the contribution of Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) derived from economic time series to the predictive performance of neural network models, specifically Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks.
papers.core_contribution: The study demonstrates that the last IMFs, representing long-term trends, are the most influential for prediction according to DeepSHAP, while high-frequency IMFs contribute less and may introduce noise. It also shows that LSTM networks distribute importance more evenly across IMFs compared to MLPs.
papers.conclusion: DeepSHAP provides a robust and effective tool for interpreting the contribution of individual IMFs in neural network–based prediction models, highlighting how both model architecture and IMF characteristics affect forecasting performance.
papers.key_findings:
The last IMFs (representing long-term trends) are generally the most influential for prediction.
High-frequency IMFs (the initial ones) contribute less predictive information and may introduce noise.
LSTM networks allocate importance more evenly across IMFs compared to MLP networks, which concentrate importance on the last IMFs.
DeepSHAP is an effective tool for interpreting the contribution of individual IMFs in neural network-based prediction models.
The model architecture (MLP vs. LSTM) affects the distribution of feature relevance across the IMF components.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the contribution of Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) derived from economic time series to the predictive performance of neural network models, specifically Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. To enhance interpretability, DeepSHAP is applied, which estimates the marginal contribution of each IMF while keeping the rest of the series intact. Results show that the last IMFs, representing long-term trends, are generally the most influential according to DeepSHAP, whereas high-frequency IMFs contribute less and may even introduce noise, as evidenced by improved metrics upon their removal. Differences between MLP and LSTM highlight the effect of model architecture on feature relevance distribution, with LSTM allocating importance more evenly across IMFs.

papers.title: Dynamics of reservoir computing for crises prediction
papers.research_question: How does reservoir computing predict crises (discontinuous transitions) in dynamical systems? Specifically, what is the mechanism behind its successful prediction of boundary and attractor-merging crises?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a trained reservoir computing map can capture crises phenomena (boundary and attractor-merging crises) and reproduce the correct scaling behavior of transient lifetimes near the crisis point by mimicking the collision of chaotic attractors with unstable fixed points, as in the original dynamical system.
papers.conclusion: Reservoir computing can capture subtle transitions in chaotic dynamics, replicating crises phenomena and recovering the correct scaling behavior, but analyzing the mechanism in higher-dimensional systems presents significant challenges.
papers.key_findings:
The trained reservoir map reproduces attractor collisions with unstable fixed points, mimicking the actual system's crisis mechanism.
The reservoir learns the quadratic nonlinearity and invariant density responsible for the observed scaling behavior near the crisis point.
The trained reservoir correctly predicts the scaling exponent of the original system (e.g., logistic map, Gauss map).
The mechanism of crisis prediction via collision with unstable fixed points holds across distinct one-dimensional systems (logistic and Gauss maps).
In higher-dimensional systems (e.g., Hénon map), the crisis mechanism is more intricate and visualization of manifolds becomes challenging, though the reservoir still reproduces the crisis.
papers.limitation: Challenges in analyzing higher-dimensional systems due to difficulty in visualizing stable and unstable manifolds and identifying periodic orbits.
future_direction: Developing strategies to overcome the challenges of analyzing higher-dimensional systems to gain deeper insight into how data-driven models capture the mechanisms of discontinuous transitions.
papers.abstract: Reservoir computing has emerged as a powerful framework for time series modelling and forecasting including the prediction of discontinuous transitions. However, the mechanism behind its success is not yet fully understood. This letter elucidates the functioning of reservoir computing by examining its successful prediction of boundary and attractor merging crises. We investigate in detail how reservoirs's internal dynamics mimic the actual system, that enables it to accurately reproduce the scaling exponent near boundary crisis. We establish this across distinct systems, exemplified by the logistic and Gauss maps. The study contributes to the broader understanding of the internal dynamics that enable learning algorithms to anticipate critical transitions.

papers.title: Internal Representations in Spiking Neural Networks, criticality and the Renormalization Group
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of a spiking neural network show signatures of criticality, such as power-law distributions, when performing classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that broad-tailed fluctuations in internal representations of spiking neural networks during input transitions are not signatures of criticality but rather arise from shifting basins of attraction, analogous to non-critical systems like an Ising model with changing external field.
papers.conclusion: Persistent fluctuations in internal representations arise from the search for new basins of attraction when the environment changes, and this is not a signature of criticality but rather a dynamical effect of changing inputs.
papers.key_findings:
Broad-tailed distributions of internal representation fluctuations occur when the network input changes category, indicated by increased correlation decay times.
These broad tails are present even when the network is partially trained or under simulated anesthesia, indicating they are not dependent on successful classification.
Avalanche size and duration distributions do not show clear power laws, suggesting the system is not critical.
The fluctuations are analogous to those in a non-critical Langevin dynamics model with time-dependent potential and in an Ising model with slowly changing external field.
Renormalization group analysis shows that large susceptibility peaks during transitions occur even away from criticality, and renormalization acts as a classifier that sharpens transitions.
papers.limitation:
Power law fits for avalanche size and duration are sensitive to choices of minimum and maximum values, and the uncertainty is larger than reported, making it impossible to affirm power laws are present.
The model of anesthesia is simplistic, acting only on the input layer by scaling pixels, and is not a realistic model of anesthesia effects.
Feed-forward neural networks are not models of the brain, limiting direct biological relevance.
papers.abstract: Optimal information processing in peripheral sensory systems has been associated in several examples to the signature of a critical or near critical state. Furthermore, cortical systems have also been described to be in a critical state in both wake and anesthetized experimental models, both {\it in vitro} and {\it in vivo}. We investigate whether a similar signature characterizes the internal representations (IR) of a multilayer (deep) spiking artificial neural network performing computationally simple but meaningful cognitive tasks, using a methodology inspired in the biological setup, with cortical implanted electrodes in rats, either freely behaving or under different levels of anesthesia. The increase of the characteristic time of the decay of the correlation of fluctuations of the IR, found when the network input changes, are indications of a broad-tailed distribution of IR fluctuations. The broad tails are present even when the network is not yet capable of performing the classification tasks, either due to partial training or to the effect of a low dose of anesthesia in a simple model. However, we don't find enough evidence of power law distributions of avalanche size and duration. We interpret the results from a renormalization group perspective to point out that despite having broad tails, this is not related to a critical transition but rather similar to fluctuations driven by the reversal of the magnetic field in a ferromagnetic system. Another example of persistent correlation of fluctuations of a non critical system is constructed, where a particle undergoes Brownian motion on a slowly varying potential.

papers.title: SOM-VAE: Interpretable Discrete Representation Learning on Time Series
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable discrete representations of time series that are smooth and provide superior clustering performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SOM-VAE, a framework for learning interpretable discrete representations of time series, featuring a gradient-based self-organizing map and an integrated Markov model for temporal smoothness and improved clustering.
papers.conclusion: SOM-VAE can recover topologically interpretable state representations on time series and static data, improves clustering performance over standard methods, and offers interpretable visualizations that could aid in domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
SOM-VAE outperforms baselines like k-means, VQ-VAE, and traditional SOM in clustering performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST in terms of purity and NMI.
The gradient-based SOM training (GB-SOM) performs better than the original SOM algorithm.
The probabilistic Markov model can be learned concurrently with the SOM-VAE and improves clustering performance on noisy data, such as medical time series.
On the chaotic Lorenz system, SOM-VAE learns interpretable representations that capture the macro-states (attractor basins) while ignoring chaotic noise.
On real medical data from the eICU database, SOM-VAE-prob learns representations that are informative for downstream prediction tasks and provides interpretable visualizations of patient trajectories.
future_direction: Extend the probabilistic component for predictions using higher-order Markov Models, Hidden Markov Models, or Gaussian Processes.
Find more theoretically principled ways to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning.
Learn the neighborhood structure as a graph directly from data instead of fixing a latent space structure like a 2D grid.
papers.abstract: High-dimensional time series are common in many domains. Since human cognition is not optimized to work well in high-dimensional spaces, these areas could benefit from interpretable low-dimensional representations. However, most representation learning algorithms for time series data are difficult to interpret. This is due to non-intuitive mappings from data features to salient properties of the representation and non-smoothness over time. To address this problem, we propose a new representation learning framework building on ideas from interpretable discrete dimensionality reduction and deep generative modeling. This framework allows us to learn discrete representations of time series, which give rise to smooth and interpretable embeddings with superior clustering performance. We introduce a new way to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning and present a gradient-based version of the traditional self-organizing map algorithm that is more performant than the original. Furthermore, to allow for a probabilistic interpretation of our method, we integrate a Markov model in the representation space. This model uncovers the temporal transition structure, improves clustering performance even further and provides additional explanatory insights as well as a natural representation of uncertainty. We evaluate our model in terms of clustering performance and interpretability on static (Fashion-)MNIST data, a time series of linearly interpolated (Fashion-)MNIST images, a chaotic Lorenz attractor system with two macro states, as well as on a challenging real world medical time series application on the eICU data set. Our learned representations compare favorably with competitor methods and facilitate downstream tasks on the real world data.

papers.title: CNN-TFT explained by SHAP with multi-head attention weights for time series forecasting
papers.research_question: How can we design a hybrid CNN-transformer architecture for time series forecasting that is both accurate and interpretable by combining SHAP with multi-head attention weights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN-transformer architecture (CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW) for multivariate time series forecasting that integrates convolutional feature extraction with a temporal fusion transformer and a novel explainability method combining SHAP with multi-head attention weights, demonstrating improved accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW model effectively captures both local patterns and long-range dependencies in time series data, providing accurate and interpretable forecasts suitable for real-world applications such as hydroelectric power planning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW model achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) as low as 2.2% on a hydroelectric natural flow dataset.
The model outperforms several state-of-the-art deep learning models (e.g., LSTM, GRU, TFT) for short-term forecasting horizons (15, 30, 60 steps ahead).
For a longer horizon (120 steps ahead), the NBEATSx model performs slightly better (0.92% lower RMSE).
Statistical analysis over 50 runs shows the model is robust with low variability in error metrics.
The combined SHAP and attention weights provide interpretable influence maps, highlighting which past time steps most affect the forecast.
future_direction: Integration of external knowledge sources
Enhanced interpretability modules
Real-time deployment frameworks
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures offer strengths for modeling temporal data: CNNs excel at capturing local patterns and translational invariances, while transformers effectively model long-range dependencies via self-attention. This paper proposes a hybrid architecture integrating convolutional feature extraction with a temporal fusion transformer (TFT) backbone to enhance multivariate time series forecasting. The CNN module first applies a hierarchy of one-dimensional convolutional layers to distill salient local patterns from raw input sequences, reducing noise and dimensionality. The resulting feature maps are then fed into the TFT, which applies multi-head attention to capture both short- and long-term dependencies and to weigh relevant covariates adaptively. We evaluate the CNN-TFT on a hydroelectric natural flow time series dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that CNN-TFT outperforms well-established deep learning models, with a mean absolute percentage error of up to 2.2%. The explainability of the model is obtained by a proposed Shapley additive explanations with multi-head attention weights (SHAP-MHAW). Our novel architecture, named CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW, is promising for applications requiring high-fidelity, multivariate time series forecasts, being available for future analysis at https://github.com/SFStefenon/CNN-TFT-SHAP-MHAW .

papers.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Autoregressive Deep Learning: Or, Examining Temporal Decay of Gradient Coherence
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish between genuine generalization and mere memorization in autoregressive PDE emulators? What are the limitations of standard models and training routines in achieving generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces influence-based diagnostics to show that autoregressive PDE emulators fail to learn a globally consistent solution operator, instead memorizing time- and class-specific patterns, and provides insights for improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current physics-agnostic PDE emulators fail to internalize the governing equations, and influence functions provide a diagnostic framework to distinguish memorization from generalization, highlighting the need for physics-based constraints or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive PDE emulators exhibit rapid decay of off-diagonal influence, indicating gradient responses are localized in time and class.
Both UNet and ViT models fail to support nontrivial off-diagonal response, meaning they do not learn a shared feature basis across trajectories.
Gradient geometry is class-locked, with limited inter-class influence, showing that models treat different initial conditions as separate tasks.
The neural tangent kernel spectrum reveals a stiff, anisotropic geometry, indicating that low test error coexists with sharp, high-curvature directions rather than robust generalization.
The models behave as statistical estimators that interpolate within neighborhoods of the training data, rather than learning the underlying physical laws.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based constraints as regularizers or architectural biases to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained as autoregressive PDE surrogates hold significant promise for accelerating scientific discovery through their capacity to both extrapolate beyond training regimes and efficiently adapt to downstream tasks despite a paucity of examples for fine-tuning. However, reliably achieving genuine generalization - a necessary capability for producing novel scientific insights and robustly performing during deployment - remains a critical challenge. Establishing whether or not these requirements are met demands evaluation metrics capable of clearly distinguishing genuine model generalization from mere memorization. We apply the influence function formalism to systematically characterize how autoregressive PDE surrogates assimilate and propagate information derived from diverse physical scenarios, revealing fundamental limitations of standard models and training routines in addition to providing actionable insights regarding the design of improved surrogates.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Linear Latent World Models in Simple Transformers: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How does Othello-GPT encode and utilize a linear world model for decision-making in the game of Othello?
papers.core_contribution: Othello-GPT encodes a linear representation of the board state in its activations, and this representation is causally utilized for next-move predictions, with the world model finalized in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: Othello-GPT neurons encode board state information linearly, and this representation is used causally for decision-making in deep networks, with the world model finalized in middle layers.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT linearly encodes board state information in its activations, with accuracy increasing in deeper layers.
Causal interventions demonstrate that the linear world model is used for next-move predictions, particularly in middle layers.
Attention heads can be categorized into types such as 'my token' and 'their token' heads, which track player moves.
Even 1-layer models can encode linear board states, but only deeper models use this information causally for decision-making.
The linear world model is fully developed in middle layers, and later layers may rely on surface statistics.
papers.limitation: Causal interventions are only successful in middle layers and early games, and may not apply to late games where the model might rely on surface statistics.
future_direction: Using mechanistic interpretability tools to understand circuits and decision-making in Othello-GPT.
papers.abstract: Foundation models exhibit significant capabilities in decision-making and logical deductions.
