papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Navigating the Latent Space Dynamics of Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can neural models, specifically autoencoders, be interpreted as dynamical systems, and what properties of the model and data can be revealed by the latent vector field and its attractors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that autoencoders implicitly define a latent vector field whose attractors encode model properties, enabling analysis of generalization and memorization, data-free probing of pretrained models, and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.conclusion: The latent vector field provides a novel and powerful representation for analyzing neural models, revealing internal properties and enabling applications like data-free probing and OOD detection.
papers.key_findings:
Autoencoders define a latent vector field whose attractors correspond to memorized data points or generalized representations, depending on regularization.
During training, the model transitions from memorization to generalization, which is reflected in the evolution of attractors.
Attractors computed from Gaussian noise can recover semantic information from pretrained vision foundation models without any input data.
Trajectories in the latent vector field can distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples, enabling OOD detection.
The memorization-generalization trade-off is controlled by regularization strength, such as bottleneck dimension.
papers.limitation: The method is primarily demonstrated on autoencoders; extension to other architectures (e.g., SSL models, LLMs) requires further analysis.
future_direction: Study latent vector fields in models beyond autoencoders, such as self-supervised learning models and large language models.
Investigate the impact of architectural elements (e.g., positional embeddings) on the latent dynamics.
Explore the connection between latent dynamics and reasoning in models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks transform high-dimensional data into compact, structured representations, often modeled as elements of a lower dimensional latent space. In this paper, we present an alternative interpretation of neural models as dynamical systems acting on the latent manifold. Specifically, we show that autoencoder models implicitly define a latent vector field on the manifold, derived by iteratively applying the encoding-decoding map, without any additional training. We observe that standard training procedures introduce inductive biases that lead to the emergence of attractor points within this vector field. Drawing on this insight, we propose to leverage the vector field as a representation for the network, providing a novel tool to analyze the properties of the model and the data. This representation enables to: (i) analyze the generalization and memorization regimes of neural models, even throughout training; (ii) extract prior knowledge encoded in the network's parameters from the attractors, without requiring any input data; (iii) identify out-of-distribution samples from their trajectories in the vector field. We further validate our approach on vision foundation models, showcasing the applicability and effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Promoting cross-modal representations to improve multimodal foundation models for physiological signals
papers.research_question: Which pretraining strategies are most effective for multimodal foundation models with diverse physiological signals, and how can cross-modal representation learning be encouraged?
papers.core_contribution: Adding input modality drop to multimodal masked autoencoding (MultiMAE) pretraining improves cross-modal representation learning and downstream task performance for diverse physiological signals.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal foundation models are effective for physiological signals, and explicitly promoting cross-modal reconstruction through input modality drop improves representation quality and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained multimodal models develop representations that support a diverse set of downstream tasks in physiological data.
Adding input modality drop to MAE pretraining improves downstream task performance compared to standard MultiMAE.
Late fusion models pretrained with contrastive learning objectives are more variable in performance and underperform MAE with modality drop on aggregate.
MAE with input modality drop encourages cross-modal fusion in attention weights and leads to more distributed tuning of embedding units across modalities.
The learned representations are effective even with limited labeled data.
papers.limitation: Making comparisons with other datasets would be additionally informative, since multimodal fusion strategies are often dependent on the dataset and task at hand.
future_direction: Developing a large range of downstream tasks to better understand the strengths of different pretraining strategies.
Developing new formulations of contrastive learning that may improve task performance for multimodal biosignals.
papers.abstract: Many healthcare applications are inherently multimodal, involving several physiological signals. As sensors for these signals become more common, improving machine learning methods for multimodal healthcare data is crucial. Pretraining foundation models is a promising avenue for success. However, methods for developing foundation models in healthcare are still in early exploration and it is unclear which pretraining strategies are most effective given the diversity of physiological signals. This is partly due to challenges in multimodal health data: obtaining data across many patients is difficult and costly, there is a lot of inter-subject variability, and modalities are often heterogeneously informative across downstream tasks. Here, we explore these challenges in the PhysioNet 2018 dataset. We use a masked autoencoding objective to pretrain a multimodal model. We show that the model learns representations that can be linearly probed for a diverse set of downstream tasks. We hypothesize that cross-modal reconstruction objectives are important for successful multimodal training, as they encourage the model to integrate information across modalities. We demonstrate that modality dropout in the input space improves performance across downstream tasks. We also find that late-fusion models pretrained with contrastive learning objectives are less effective across multiple tasks. Finally, we analyze the model's representations, showing that attention weights become more cross-modal and temporally aligned with our pretraining strategy. The learned embeddings also become more distributed in terms of the modalities encoded by each unit. Overall, our work demonstrates the utility of multimodal foundation models with health data, even across diverse physiological data sources. We further argue that explicit methods for inducing cross-modality may enhance multimodal pretraining strategies.

papers.title: When can isotropy help adapt LLMs' next word prediction to numerical domains?
papers.research_question: When (or how) can the next-word prediction capability of LLMs be effectively adapted to numerical domains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that isotropy in the contextual embedding space of LLMs stabilizes the partition function, resolves the shift-invariance problem of softmax, and provides performance guarantees for numerical downstream tasks like time series forecasting.
papers.conclusion: Isotropy in LLM hidden representations stabilizes the partition function and enables better generalization in numerical downstream tasks, serving as a reliable indicator of structured representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
The isotropy of LLM hidden representations varies based on input data characteristics (domain, context length, noise) and model design choices (tokenization, architecture), which directly influences forecasting performance.
The self-attention mechanism implicitly aligns with the dominant eigenvectors of the input correlation structure, inducing isotropy in the contextual embedding space.
Isotropy stabilizes the partition function, enabling better generalization in numerical downstream tasks across different models and datasets.
papers.limitation: While isotropy offers a principled way to preserve useful structure, there may be alternative approaches to approximating the partition function and guiding numerical reasoning.
future_direction: Developing mechanisms to recover or enhance structure when isotropy is weak.
papers.abstract: Vector representations of contextual embeddings learned by pre-trained large language models (LLMs) are effective in various downstream tasks in numerical domains such as time series forecasting. Despite their significant benefits, the tendency of LLMs to hallucinate in such domains can have severe consequences in applications such as energy, nature, finance, healthcare, retail and transportation, among others. To guarantee prediction reliability and accuracy in numerical domains, it is necessary to open the black box behind the LLM and provide performance guarantees through explanation. However, there is little theoretical understanding of when pre-trained language models help solve numerical downstream tasks. This paper seeks to bridge this gap by understanding when the next-word prediction capability of LLMs can be adapted to numerical domains through a novel analysis based on the concept of isotropy in the contextual embedding space. Specifically, a log-linear model for LLMs is considered in which numerical data can be predicted from its context through a network with softmax in the output layer of LLMs (i.e., language model head in self-attention). For this model, it is demonstrated that, in order to achieve state-of-the-art performance in numerical domains, the hidden representations of the LLM embeddings must possess a structure that accounts for the shift-invariance of the softmax function. By formulating a gradient structure of self-attention in pre-trained models, it is shown how the isotropic property of LLM embeddings in contextual embedding space preserves the underlying structure of representations, thereby resolving the shift-invariance problem and providing a performance guarantee. Experiments show that different characteristics of numerical data and model architectures have different impacts on isotropy, and this variability directly affects the performances.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Same Answer, Different Representations: Hidden instability in VLMs
papers.research_question: Does output-level robustness in VLMs mask representation drift? Specifically, do VLMs maintain predictions under image perturbations while exhibiting representation drift?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a representation-aware and frequency-aware evaluation framework for VLMs, revealing that output-level robustness often masks significant internal representation drift under perturbations.
papers.conclusion: The findings challenge the assumption that high base accuracy or increased model scale reliably confer robustness, and show that robustness evaluation must extend beyond output accuracy to include representation stability and structural smoothness.
papers.key_findings:
Models frequently preserve predicted answers while undergoing substantial internal representation drift; for perturbations such as text overlays, this drift approaches the magnitude of inter-image variability.
Robustness does not improve with scale; larger models achieve higher accuracy but exhibit equal or greater sensitivity.
Perturbations affect tasks differently: they harm reasoning when they disrupt how models combine coarse and fine visual cues, but on hallucination benchmarks, they can reduce false positives by making models generate more conservative answers.
Text overlays are particularly disruptive, inducing the largest representation drift and flip rates.
Perturbations induce both error injection (correct to wrong) and correction (wrong to correct) transitions, indicating bidirectional movement across decision boundaries.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a specific set of vision-language models and benchmarks, which may not fully capture the diversity of architectures and task distributions in deployment.
Frequency-domain analysis relies on specific metrics (Dirichlet energy, spectral norms) that may not capture all aspects of representational drift.
papers.abstract: The robustness of Vision Language Models (VLMs) is commonly assessed through output-level invariance, implicitly assuming that stable predictions reflect stable multimodal processing. In this work, we argue that this assumption is insufficient. We introduce a representation-aware and frequency-aware evaluation framework that measures internal embedding drift, spectral sensitivity, and structural smoothness (spatial consistency of vision tokens), alongside standard label-based metrics. Applying this framework to modern VLMs across the SEEDBench, MMMU, and POPE datasets reveals three distinct failure modes. First, models frequently preserve predicted answers while undergoing substantial internal representation drift; for perturbations such as text overlays, this drift approaches the magnitude of inter-image variability, indicating that representations move to regions typically occupied by unrelated inputs despite unchanged outputs. Second, robustness does not improve with scale; larger models achieve higher accuracy but exhibit equal or greater sensitivity, consistent with sharper yet more fragile decision boundaries. Third, we find that perturbations affect tasks differently: they harm reasoning when they disrupt how models combine coarse and fine visual cues, but on the hallucination benchmarks, they can reduce false positives by making models generate more conservative answers.

papers.title: Understanding Transformers for Time Series: Rank Structure, Flow-of-ranks, and Compressibility
papers.research_question: How well do community insights on pretraining and hyperparameter tuning, based largely on Transformers applied to text data, port to Transformers applied to other data modalities, specifically time series?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework for analyzing Transformers in time series through rank structure, showing that time-series embeddings are low-rank, which leads to compressible attention matrices, and introduces the flow-of-ranks concept to explain rank growth across layers, enabling effective compression of time series foundation models.
papers.conclusion: The rank structure framework provides principled guidance for allocating width, depth, and heads in time series foundation models and for exploiting their inherent compressibility, demonstrating significant practical compression gains.
papers.key_findings:
Time-series embeddings exhibit sharply decaying singular value spectra, making them low-rank compared to text or vision embeddings.
Attention layers on low-rank inputs admit accurate low-rank approximations, making them compressible.
Flow-of-ranks describes how nonlinear mixing across depth inflates rank, explaining why early layers are more compressible and ranks grow with depth.
Time series foundation models are highly compressible compared to language models of the same size.
Compressing Chronos reduces inference time by 65.4% and memory usage by 81.4% without loss of accuracy.
future_direction: Sparse parameterization of sketching matrices in head-dependent low-rank representations.
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely used across data modalities, and yet the principles distilled from text models often transfer imperfectly to models trained to other modalities. In this paper, we analyze Transformers through the lens of rank structure. Our focus is on the time series setting, where the structural properties of the data differ remarkably from those of text or vision. We show that time-series embeddings, unlike text or vision, exhibit sharply decaying singular value spectra: small patch sizes and smooth continuous mappings concentrate the data into low-rank subspaces. From this, we prove that the associated $Q/K/V$ projections admit accurate low-rank approximations, and that attention layers become compressible in proportion to the decay of the embedding spectrum. We introduce the concept of flow-of-ranks, a phenomenon by which nonlinear mixing across depth inflates the rank, explaining why early layers are most amenable to compression and why ranks grow with depth. Guided by these theoretical and empirical results, we use these insights to compress Chronos, a large time series foundation model, achieving a reduction of $65\%$ in inference time and $81\%$ in memory, without loss of accuracy. Our findings provide principled guidance for allocating width, depth, and heads in time series foundation models, and for exploiting their inherent compressibility.

papers.title: Explainable deep learning for rainfall prediction: A CNN-XGBoost hybrid approach in the northern region of Bangladesh
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the application of deep learning models for rainfall prediction in the northern region of Bangladesh, focusing on the comparative performance of six models and the interpretability of a proposed hybrid model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN-XGBoost model for rainfall prediction that consistently outperforms other models (CNN, LSTM, XGB, Ensemble, Transformer-XGB) across two distinct datasets and provides interpretability of its decisions using SHAP.
papers.conclusion: The CNN-XGB hybrid model provides accurate and consistent rainfall predictions for the northern region of Bangladesh, outperforming other models, and the use of SHAP enhances model transparency and trust for practical applications like urban planning and disaster management.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN-XGB hybrid model achieved the lowest RMSE (0.65 mm/day) and MAE (0.28 mm/day) and highest R2 (0.99) on the satellite dataset for Rajshahi district.
On the ground dataset, the CNN-XGB model also performed best for Rajshahi district with RMSE of 16.28 mm/month, MAE of 7.85 mm/month, and R2 of 0.98.
The satellite dataset with 16 meteorological variables led to better model performance than the ground dataset with only rainfall data.
SHAP analysis identified that engineered features (e.g., trends, rolling statistics, transformations of precipitation) and climatic variables were the most influential predictors.
The hybrid model effectively captures both spatial and temporal patterns in rainfall data, demonstrating robustness across different districts and data sources.
papers.limitation:
The ground dataset's monthly resolution restricts the model's ability to capture short-term rainfall variability.
Crucial environmental and urban factors such as soil moisture, land use, and topography were excluded due to data unavailability, which may affect localized accuracy.
future_direction: Explore domain adaptation to improve generalization across diverse regions.
Integrate multi-source data (e.g., radar observations, vegetation indices, satellite-derived soil moisture) to enhance robustness under varying climatic conditions.
Couple the proposed model with numerical weather prediction (NWP) models to refine forecasts by blending data-driven and physics-based approaches.
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate precipitation forecasting is crucial for evaluating various hydrological processes. This research explores the application of deep learning models for rainfall prediction in the northern region of Bangladesh, focusing on the comparative performance of six models: CNN (Convolutional Neural Network), LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), XGB (Extreme Gradient Boosting), Ensemble Model, Transformer-XGB, and CNN-XGB. Two distinct datasets were utilized to assess the effectiveness of these models. Among them, the CNN-XGB hybrid model consistently demonstrated superior performance across all evaluation metrics, establishing it as the most reliable predictor in this study. Rajshahi district’s satellite dataset showed an RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) of 0.65 mm/day, MAE (Mean Absolute Error) of 0.28 mm/day, and R 2 of 0.99. In the ground dataset, Rajshahi district beat other models with an RMSE of 16.28 mm/month, MAE of 7.85 mm/month, and R 2 of 0.98. These findings demonstrate the model’s efficacy across several data sources. To enhance the interpretability of the proposed CNN-XGB model, we deployed the SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) explainer, providing insights into the model’s decision-making process. This research highlights the potential of hybrid models in enhancing rainfall prediction accuracy while providing transparency through explainable AI techniques. Beyond hydrology, the predicted rainfall patterns provide essential inputs for urban planners to optimize land-use zoning in flood-prone areas, and guide resilient infrastructure development. Code Available: https://github.com/Shafi3397/Rainfall-Prediction-using-CNN-XGBoost

papers.title: Ability Transfer and Recovery via Modularized Parameters Localization
papers.research_question: How are abilities distributed within LLM parameters? The paper investigates this by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ACT, a method that localizes ability-relevant channels in LLMs via cross-model activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, enabling efficient ability transfer and recovery while minimizing interference.
papers.conclusion: ACT enables efficient and effective ability transfer and recovery by localizing and transferring modularized ability-relevant parameters, and it can integrate multiple abilities into a single model with minimal interference.
papers.key_findings:
Large activation differences are concentrated in a small fraction of channels (typically <5%).
Activation difference distributions across different layers exhibit consistent heavy-tailed patterns.
Ability-specific channels are naturally disentangled across different language-domain abilities.
Ability-specific channels exhibit consistency after fine-tuning across different fine-tuned variants.
Ability-specific channels selected by activations differ from largely updated ones during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes the availability of a base model and an ability model that share the same architecture and tokenizer, and are preferably derived from the same pretrained checkpoint.
The effectiveness of ACT may be limited when the parameter drift between the base and ability models is too large, as observed in some continuous pre-training scenarios.
future_direction: Extending ACT to more diverse abilities and tasks beyond reasoning domains.
Exploring the theoretical foundations of activation-based ability localization.
Applying ACT to other model families and architectures beyond transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models can be continually pre-trained or fine-tuned to improve performance in specific domains, languages, or skills, but this specialization often degrades other capabilities and may cause catastrophic forgetting. We investigate how abilities are distributed within LLM parameters by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models. Across layers and modules, we find that ability-related activations are highly concentrated in a small set of channels (typically <5\%), and these channels are largely disentangled with good sufficiency and stability. Building on these observations, we propose ACT (Activation-Guided Channel-wise Ability Transfer), which localizes ability-relevant channels via activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, followed by lightweight fine-tuning for compatibility. Experiments on multilingual mathematical and scientific reasoning show that ACT can recover forgotten abilities while preserving retained skills. It can also merge multiple specialized models to integrate several abilities into a single model with minimal interference. Our code and data will be publicly released.

papers.title: Modes of Sequence Models and Learning Coefficients
papers.research_question: How does the geometry of the loss landscape, as captured by Local Learning Coefficient (LLC) estimation, relate to the modes (principal patterns) in the data distribution of sequence models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Local Learning Coefficient (LLC) estimates are insensitive to small-amplitude modes in the data distribution, meaning they effectively measure the geometry of a coarse-grained 'effective' distribution rather than the true distribution.
papers.conclusion: The modal framework provides a foundation for understanding the geometry of learning in sequence models and clarifies the role and interpretation of Local Learning Coefficient estimation.
papers.key_findings:
Sequence distributions can be decomposed into fundamental patterns (modes) using tensor decompositions in a Hilbert space framework.
Truncating small-amplitude modes yields an effective true distribution that preserves dominant structure while discarding statistical detail.
LLC estimation is theoretically insensitive to modes below a data-dependent threshold, so it characterizes the geometry of the effective distribution.
The inverse temperature parameter in Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) acts as a resolution dial on the loss landscape structure.
This explains why reliable LLC estimates can be obtained even when a parameter is not a strict minimizer of the population loss.
papers.limitation: The theoretical bounds on insensitivity constants for modern transformer architectures need to be tightened, and a more sophisticated treatment is needed for the case where the minibatch size m is small, which is how SGLD is used in practice.
future_direction: Explore alternative tensor factorizations (such as CP, Tucker, tensor-train) to capture more complex hierarchies of modes.
Tighten quantitative bounds on the insensitivity constants for modern transformer architectures.
Develop a more sophisticated treatment of the main theorems that allows keeping the minibatch size m small, consistent with practical SGLD use.
papers.abstract: We develop a geometric account of sequence modelling that links patterns in the data to measurable properties of the loss landscape in transformer networks. First, we cast conditional sequence distributions into a Hilbert-space framework and apply tensor decompositions to identify their principal modes. Truncating the small-amplitude modes yields an effective data distribution that preserves dominant structure while discarding statistical detail. Second, we show theoretically that Local Learning Coefficient (LLC) estimates are insensitive to modes below a data-dependent threshold. Consequently, the LLC calculated in practice characterises the geometry of the effective rather than the true distribution. This insight clarifies why reliable LLC estimates can be obtained even when a network parameter is not a strict minimiser of the population loss, and it highlights how the inverse temperature in SGLD acts as a resolution dial on the landscape structure.

papers.title: SourceNet: Interpretable Sim-to-Real Inference on Variable-Geometry Sensor Arrays for Earthquake Source Inversion
papers.research_question: How to infer high-dimensional physical states (earthquake source parameters) from sparse, ad-hoc sensor arrays, bridging the Sim-to-Real gap via physics-structured domain randomization.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SourceNet, a Transformer-based framework for earthquake source inversion that bridges the Sim-to-Real gap via Physics-Structured Domain Randomization (PSDR), and shows the model autonomously discovers optimal experimental design principles.
papers.conclusion: SourceNet bridges deep learning and rigorous physical inference on variable-geometry arrays, and demonstrates that interpretability can lead to discovery of physical strategies such as optimal experimental design.
papers.key_findings:
SourceNet achieves state-of-the-art precision on held-out real earthquake data, demonstrating effective Sim-to-Real transfer.
Physics-Structured Domain Randomization (PSDR) enables robust feature learning invariant to unmodeled environmental heterogeneity.
Self-attention is theoretically superior to pooling-based baselines (e.g., DeepSets) for wave physics, capturing relational dependencies.
Interpretability analysis reveals the model autonomously discovers geometric information bottlenecks and learns an attention policy that prioritizes sparse sensor placements, recovering principles of optimal experimental design.
The model uses full-waveform information, including scattered coda phases typically ignored by classical solvers.
papers.limitation: The framework assumes the simulation covers the physics of the real world, and out-of-distribution events (e.g., complex multi-fault ruptures) remain challenging.
future_direction: Extend the framework to model the full spatiotemporal evolution of fault slip using neural surrogates.
papers.abstract: Inferring high-dimensional physical states from sparse, ad-hoc sensor arrays is a fundamental challenge across AI for Science, yet standard architectures like CNNs and DeepSets struggle to capture the irregular geometries and relational physics inherent to domains like seismology. To address this, we propose SourceNet, a Transformer-based framework that bridges the profound Sim-to-Real gap via Physics-Structured Domain Randomization (PSDR), a protocol that randomizes governing physical dynamics to enforce invariance to unmodeled environmental heterogeneity. By pre-training on 100,000 synthetic events and fine-tuning on ~2,500 real-world events, SourceNet achieves state-of-the-art precision on held-out real data, demonstrating exceptional data efficiency and real-time capability compared to classical solvers. Beyond prediction, interpretability analysis reveals that the model shows scientific-agent-like features: it autonomously discovers geometric information bottlenecks and learns an attention policy that prioritizes sparse sensor placements, effectively recovering principles of optimal experimental design from data alone.

papers.title: The geometry of BERT
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention mechanism work internally, and what insights can be gained about its classification process?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel theoretical perspective on BERT's attention mechanism, introducing the concepts of directionality of subspace selection and cone index, and analyzes attention patterns and global information flow to understand its classification process.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
The attention mechanism in BERT performs a subspace selection driven by the searching engine process (Q, K, V matrices).
The self-attention matrix exhibits specific, classifiable patterns (e.g., directional gate, open gate, contextual gates) that convey different types of information.
The cone index and distribution analysis show that lower layers specialize in finding information content, while upper layers primarily propagate it.
The information content propagates globally as a mean information content; the MLP synthesizes information from different heads, breaking the channel structure.
Rank collapse in attention is reinterpreted as a potential carrier of directional information rather than a purely negative phenomenon.
future_direction: Analysis of the BERT learning process during training.
Examining the specialization of individual components in the BERT architecture.
Leveraging these findings to optimize the architecture of the Transformer encoder.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks, particularly Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), have shown remarkable performance across various tasks such as classification, text summarization, and question answering. However, their internal mechanisms remain mathematically obscure, highlighting the need for greater explainability and interpretability. In this direction, this paper investigates the internal mechanisms of BERT proposing a novel perspective on the attention mechanism of BERT from a theoretical perspective. The analysis encompasses both local and global network behavior. At the local level, the concept of directionality of subspace selection as well as a comprehensive study of the patterns emerging from the self-attention matrix are presented. Additionally, this work explores the semantic content of the information stream through data distribution analysis and global statistical measures including the novel concept of cone index. A case study on the classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants using RNA which resulted in a very high accuracy has been selected in order to observe these concepts in an application. The insights gained from this analysis contribute to a deeper understanding of BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models and further analysis in the training process.

papers.title: When and where do feed-forward neural networks learn localist representations?
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do localist representations (local codes) emerge in feed-forward parallel distributed processing (PDP) neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Localist coding can emerge in feed-forward PDP networks, and the number of local codes is influenced by network architecture, data properties, and training noise, suggesting they may offer computational efficiency and noise resilience.
papers.conclusion: Localist representations can emerge in feed-forward PDP networks under conditions such as invariant features in the data and noisy training, and may be found in middle and higher layers of deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
The number of local codes follows a well-defined distribution across hidden layer neurons, with a peak determined by input data size, number of examples, and sparsity.
Fewer training examples per class leads to more local codes.
Sparse input data (low sparseness) increases the number of local codes.
Using a 1-hot output encoding drastically reduces the number of local codes in the hidden layer.
Dropout increases the number of local codes, suggesting local codes offer resilience to noisy networks.
papers.limitation:
The data used is a simple pattern classification task, which may not reflect more complex real-world data.
Local codes only emerge when there are invariant features shared within a category.
future_direction: Investigate the qualities of data passed within a neural network to see if local codes emerge in deeper layers.
Explore whether local codes have diagnostic use for generalization or overfitting.
Test the findings on standard datasets like the Iris dataset.
papers.abstract: According to parallel distributed processing (PDP) theory in psychology, neural networks (NN) learn distributed rather than interpretable localist representations. This view has been held so strongly that few researchers have analysed single units to determine if this assumption is correct. However, recent results from psychology, neuroscience and computer science have shown the occasional existence of local codes emerging in artificial and biological neural networks. In this paper, we undertake the first systematic survey of when local codes emerge in a feed-forward neural network, using generated input and output data with known qualities. We find that the number of local codes that emerge from a NN follows a well-defined distribution across the number of hidden layer neurons, with a peak determined by the size of input data, number of examples presented and the sparsity of input data. Using a 1-hot output code drastically decreases the number of local codes on the hidden layer. The number of emergent local codes increases with the percentage of dropout applied to the hidden layer, suggesting that the localist encoding may offer a resilience to noisy networks. This data suggests that localist coding can emerge from feed-forward PDP networks and suggests some of the conditions that may lead to interpretable localist representations in the cortex. The findings highlight how local codes should not be dismissed out of hand.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Interpretable Pre-Trained Transformers for Heart Time-Series Data
papers.research_question: Can decoder-only transformers be effectively applied to physiological time-series data (PPG and ECG) to create interpretable pre-trained models that are easily fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as classification of heart conditions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two interpretable pre-trained transformer models (PPG-PT and ECG-PT) for heart time-series data, demonstrating that they can be effectively fine-tuned for tasks like atrial fibrillation classification and beat detection, while providing interpretability through attention maps and embedding analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work has conclusively demonstrated that GPT-like models, trained to predict the next token in periodic physiological time series, are fully interpretable in their operation, and this interpretability is maintained when fine-tuning for classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The models' attention mechanisms focus on similar points in previous cardiac cycles and broaden their focus in deeper layers.
Tokens with the same value but occurring at different phases form separate clusters in embedding space as they propagate through the transformer.
Individual attention heads respond to specific physiologically relevant features (e.g., dicrotic notch in PPG, P-wave in ECG).
The pre-trained models can be fine-tuned quickly (11 minutes) for atrial fibrillation classification, achieving high AUC (0.99 for ECG, 0.93 for PPG).
The fine-tuned beat detector achieves a state-of-the-art F1 score of 98% and provides beat confidence values that act as a signal quality estimator.
papers.limitation: The models are pre-trained on clinical data and may not transfer well to wearable sensor data without further training.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only transformers are the backbone of the popular generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) series of large language models. In this work, we employ this framework to the analysis of clinical heart time-series data, to create two pre-trained general purpose cardiac models, termed PPG-PT and ECG-PT. We place a special emphasis on making both such pre-trained models fully interpretable. This is achieved firstly through aggregate attention maps which show that, in order to make predictions, the model focuses on similar points in previous cardiac cycles and gradually broadens its attention in deeper layers. Next, we show that tokens with the same value, which occur at different distinct points in the electrocardiography (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG) cycle, form separate clusters in high dimensional space. The clusters form according to phase, as the tokens propagate through the transformer blocks. Finally, we highlight that individual attention heads respond to specific physiologically relevent features, such as the dicrotic notch in PPG and the P-wave in ECG. It is also demonstrated that these pre-trained models are straightforward to fine-tune for tasks such as classification of atrial fibrillation (AF), and beat detection in photoplethysmography. For the example of AF, the fine-tuning took 11 minutes of computer time, and achieved the respective leave-one-subject-out AUCs of 0.99 and 0.93 for ECG and PPG within the MIMIC Perform AF dataset. In addition, the fine-tuned beat detector achieved a state-of-the-art F1 score of 98%, as well as uniquely providing a beat confidence level which acts as a signal quality estimator. Importantly, the fine-tuned models for AF screening are also fully explainable, with attention shifting to regions in the context that are strongly indicative of atrial fibrillation.

papers.title: Analyzing Deep Transformer Models for Time Series Forecasting via Manifold Learning
papers.research_question: How do geometric features (intrinsic dimension and curvature) of latent representations in transformer-based time series forecasting models change across layers, correlate with performance, and evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer-based time series forecasting models exhibit consistent geometric profiles in their latent manifolds, with intrinsic dimension and curvature patterns that correlate with model performance, providing a new perspective for model analysis and design.
papers.conclusion: Manifold learning provides a valuable framework for analyzing transformer-based time series forecasting models, revealing geometric patterns and correlations that can guide the development of improved forecasting architectures.
papers.key_findings:
During encoding, intrinsic dimension and curvature decrease or remain fixed, while during decoding they increase.
Geometric profiles are similar across different architectures, datasets, and forecast horizons.
Mean absolute principal curvature (MAPC) in the final layer is positively correlated with test mean squared error, indicating lower error with lower curvature.
Untrained models exhibit random geometric profiles that converge rapidly within a few epochs of training.
Datasets with underlying correlations (e.g., weather and electricity transformer temperature) show similar geometric features.
future_direction: Deeper investigation of classification versus regression from a manifold learning perspective.
Design of deeper and more expressive time series forecasting models.
papers.abstract: Transformer models have consistently achieved remarkable results in various domains such as natural language processing and computer vision. However, despite ongoing research efforts to better understand these models, the field still lacks a comprehensive understanding. This is particularly true for deep time series forecasting methods, where analysis and understanding work is relatively limited. Time series data, unlike image and text information, can be more challenging to interpret and analyze. To address this, we approach the problem from a manifold learning perspective, assuming that the latent representations of time series forecasting models lie next to a low-dimensional manifold. In our study, we focus on analyzing the geometric features of these latent data manifolds, including intrinsic dimension and principal curvatures. Our findings reveal that deep transformer models exhibit similar geometric behavior across layers, and these geometric features are correlated with model performance. Additionally, we observe that untrained models initially have different structures, but they rapidly converge during training. By leveraging our geometric analysis and differentiable tools, we can potentially design new and improved deep forecasting neural networks. This approach complements existing analysis studies and contributes to a better understanding of transformer models in the context of time series forecasting. Code is released at https://github.com/azencot-group/GATLM.

papers.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the origin of the block structure phenomenon in neural network representations? Does it arise from overfitting to spurious data features or does it capture meaningful dataset statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The block structure phenomenon arises from dominant datapoints that share simple image statistics (e.g., background color), which vary across random seeds. The block structure can be eliminated via principal component regularization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The block structure captures real but simple dataset statistics, and its inconsistency across seeds is due to variation in which statistics are captured. Training interventions like principal component regularization can reduce the block structure and improve representational consistency.
papers.key_findings:
The block structure is caused by a small set of dominant datapoints that share similar image statistics (e.g., background color).
The set of dominant datapoints and the specific image statistic they capture vary across random seeds.
Removing dominant datapoints from the analysis eliminates the block structure.
The block structure emerges early in training, but the dominant datapoints and representations continue to change substantially.
Principal component regularization can eliminate the block structure and improve model consistency across seeds without hurting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Focus on image classification tasks and ResNet architectures; it remains to be seen how the block structure manifests in other domains and architectures.
Analysis is primarily empirical; a theoretical understanding is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring how dominant datapoints manifest in other domains and applications.
Applying principal component regularization to distribution shift and self-supervision problems.
papers.abstract: Recent work has uncovered a striking phenomenon in large-capacity neural networks: they contain blocks of contiguous hidden layers with highly similar representations. This block structure has two seemingly contradictory properties: on the one hand, its constituent layers exhibit highly similar dominant first principal components (PCs), but on the other hand, their representations, and their common first PC, are highly dissimilar across different random seeds. Our work seeks to reconcile these discrepant properties by investigating the origin of the block structure in relation to the data and training methods. By analyzing properties of the dominant PCs, we find that the block structure arises from dominant datapoints - a small group of examples that share similar image statistics (e.g. background color). However, the set of dominant datapoints, and the precise shared image statistic, can vary across random seeds. Thus, the block structure reflects meaningful dataset statistics, but is simultaneously unique to each model. Through studying hidden layer activations and creating synthetic datapoints, we demonstrate that these simple image statistics dominate the representational geometry of the layers inside the block structure. We explore how the phenomenon evolves through training, finding that the block structure takes shape early in training, but the underlying representations and the corresponding dominant datapoints continue to change substantially. Finally, we study the interplay between the block structure and different training mechanisms, introducing a targeted intervention to eliminate the block structure, as well as examining the effects of pretraining and Shake-Shake regularization.

papers.title: Representing Neural Network Layers as Linear Operations via Koopman Operator Theory
papers.research_question: Can we linearize individual layers of a neural network using Koopman operator theory and delay-coordinates embedding, and how does this affect model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to linearize individual layers of a neural network using Koopman operator theory and delay-coordinates embedding, achieving performance close to the original network.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Koopman theory and delay-coordinates embedding can linearize individual neural network layers while retaining performance, offering a new perspective for understanding and controlling networks.
papers.key_findings:
Delay-coordinates embedding (Hankelization) is an effective observable function for linearizing neural network layers via Koopman theory.
Replacing layers with a linear DMD model retains high accuracy: up to 97.3% on Yin-Yang (vs 98.4% original) and up to 95.8% on MNIST (vs 97.2% original).
The success of layer replacement varies by layer; replacing the final hidden layer is most successful, suggesting it performs a simpler transformation.
Increasing the delay parameter and number of trajectories improves the DMD model's performance.
Eigenvalue and singular vector analysis shows that delay embedding linearizes the dynamics, as seen in simpler sinusoidal patterns in singular vectors.
papers.limitation: The maximum delay parameter is limited by the number of scaling layers, which restricts the exploration of delay parameters.
future_direction: Analyze the learned eigenmodes and eigenvalues to understand their relationship with layer replacement success.
Develop methods to edit trained models in the Koopman space.
Extend the framework to other architectures like convolutional or attention layers.
papers.abstract: The strong performance of simple neural networks is often attributed to their nonlinear activations. However, a linear view of neural networks makes understanding and controlling networks much more approachable. We draw from a dynamical systems view of neural networks, offering a fresh perspective by using Koopman operator theory and its connections with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). Together, they offer a framework for linearizing dynamical systems by embedding the system into an appropriate observable space. By reframing a neural network as a dynamical system, we demonstrate that we can replace the nonlinear layer in a pretrained multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a finite-dimensional linear operator. In addition, we analyze the eigenvalues of DMD and the right singular vectors of SVD, to present evidence that time-delayed coordinates provide a straightforward and highly effective observable space for Koopman theory to linearize a network layer. Consequently, we replace layers of an MLP trained on the Yin-Yang dataset with predictions from a DMD model, achieving a mdoel accuracy of up to 97.3%, compared to the original 98.4%. In addition, we replace layers in an MLP trained on the MNIST dataset, achieving up to 95.8%, compared to the original 97.2% on the test set.

papers.title: Foundation Model's Embedded Representations May Detect Distribution Shift
papers.research_question: How can foundation models' embedded representations detect distribution shift, and how does fine-tuning under such shift affect generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: Foundation models' embedded representations can detect distribution shift between train and test sets via PCA, and linear probing on pre-trained features may outperform fine-tuning when such shift exists, emphasizing the importance of data alignment for generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that foundation models' embeddings can detect distribution shift, and that fine-tuning under shift may harm performance, advocating for data sampling from the same population and considering linear probing when pre-trained features are sufficient.
papers.key_findings:
PCA on final layer embeddings visually separates datasets P and M, confirming distribution shift.
Fine-tuning on the automatically labeled dataset P leads to worse performance on the manually curated dataset M compared to linear probing on M.
Linear probes on pre-trained features are robust and can achieve high accuracy with less data and computational cost.
The ability to discern distribution shift correlates with model complexity or size, as larger models show better separation.
Training on misaligned data can confound model interpretation and generalization assessment, suggesting caution in transfer learning.
papers.limitation:
The approach is an ad hoc qualitative measure for detecting distribution shifts, not a principled test statistic.
The correlation between model complexity and ability to discern shift is not causal and may be confounded by other factors like pre-training data.
future_direction: Developing quantitative hypothesis testing for distribution shift detection based on model architecture and data.
Investigating the causal factors behind models' ability to discern distribution shift.
papers.abstract: Sampling biases can cause distribution shifts between train and test datasets for supervised learning tasks, obscuring our ability to understand the generalization capacity of a model. This is especially important considering the wide adoption of pre-trained foundational neural networks -- whose behavior remains poorly understood -- for transfer learning (TL) tasks. We present a case study for TL on the Sentiment140 dataset and show that many pre-trained foundation models encode different representations of Sentiment140's manually curated test set $M$ from the automatically labeled training set $P$, confirming that a distribution shift has occurred. We argue training on $P$ and measuring performance on $M$ is a biased measure of generalization. Experiments on pre-trained GPT-2 show that the features learnable from $P$ do not improve (and in fact hamper) performance on $M$. Linear probes on pre-trained GPT-2's representations are robust and may even outperform overall fine-tuning, implying a fundamental importance for discerning distribution shift in train/test splits for model interpretation.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Dataset-learning duality and emergent criticality
